questions.question: What are the three topics listed in the 'This chapter covers' box?
questions.answer: Generating text with a deep learning model; training a model to translate English to Spanish; the Transformer architecture for text modeling.
questions.explanation: Taken directly from the box on this page.

questions.question: Why do the authors call text classification 'a uniquely simple problem'?
questions.answer: Its output is tiny and fixed: one float for binary classification or N numbers for N-way classification. Generation has to produce a sequence chosen from an exponentially large space.
questions.explanation: Stated in section 15.1 on this page; the size of the generation space is quantified on p.446.

questions.question: Which product does the chapter introduction mention as being powered by the Transformer?
options: Google Translate
ChatGPT
Siri
AlphaGo
questions.answer: ChatGPT
questions.explanation: The introduction says the Transformer 'powers products like ChatGPT'. The other products are not mentioned on this page.

questions.question: Before reading on: how would you design a model whose output is a sentence rather than a label? Write down your idea and compare it with p.446.
questions.answer: Open-ended; the book's answer is to predict one token at a time with p(token | past tokens) and repeat.
questions.explanation: Thinking about this first makes the language-model framing easier to absorb.

questions.question: How does the pretraining idea from the end of Chapter 14 relate to this chapter?
questions.answer: Language modeling is an unsupervised task on unlabeled text, the same kind of pretraining task Chapter 14 used CBOW for, but applied to whole models such as the Transformer encoder that is fine-tuned on IMDb in section 15.4.
questions.explanation: See p.444 for the pretraining summary and p.478-479 for pretraining a Transformer encoder.

questions.question: With a vocabulary of 20,000 words, how many possible 3-word sequences are there, and how many outputs does a language model need per prediction step?
questions.answer: 20,000^3 = 8 x 10^12 (8 trillion) sequences; a language model needs only 20,000 outputs per step.
questions.explanation: Each position has 20,000 choices, so the count is V^L. The language model predicts one token, so its output size is V.

questions.question: What distribution does a language model learn in its simplest form, according to the page?
options: p(past tokens | token)
p(token | past tokens)
p(token | surrounding tokens)
p(label | entire sequence)
questions.answer: p(token | past tokens)
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. p(token | surrounding tokens) is the masked language model (p.479). p(label | sequence) is classification. The first option reverses the conditioning.

questions.question: Why is a direct classifier over all output sequences intractable even with unlimited model design freedom?
questions.answer: The number of classes grows exponentially (V^L). For 20 words it exceeds the number of atoms in the universe, so no output layer could represent each sequence and there would never be training data for almost all classes.
questions.explanation: The page says this 'would overwhelm compute resources no matter how we design our model.'

questions.question: What does it mean to detokenize a sequence?
questions.answer: Map each integer ID back to its string token and join the tokens together, the reverse of tokenization.
questions.explanation: Defined in the second paragraph of the page; used on p.451.

questions.question: In Listing 15.1, what does keras.utils.get_file return, and what is stored in the variable shakespeare?
questions.answer: get_file returns the local path of the downloaded (cached) file; shakespeare holds the entire file contents as a single string.
questions.explanation: open(filename, 'r').read() reads the whole text into memory.

questions.question: How can a model that predicts only one token produce a long passage?
questions.answer: By repeatedly predicting the next token, appending it to the context, and predicting again. Each step's output becomes part of the next step's input.
questions.explanation: The page says 'by repeatedly predicting the next token, we will have built a model that can generate a long sequence of text'; implemented on p.450.

questions.question: Can you verify the claim about 20-word sequences and atoms in the universe using powers of ten?
questions.answer: 20,000^20 = 2^20 x 10^80, about 1.05 x 10^86, which exceeds the roughly 10^80 atoms usually estimated.
questions.explanation: Write 20,000 = 2 x 10^4 and raise it to the 20th power.

questions.question: In Listing 15.2, why are features built from shakespeare[:-1] and labels from shakespeare[1:]?
options: To remove the header and footer of the file
So that each label sequence is the feature sequence offset by one character
To make the dataset size a multiple of 100
To produce overlapping windows for data augmentation
questions.answer: So that each label sequence is the feature sequence offset by one character
questions.explanation: Chunking both slices at the same offsets aligns label t with character t+1. The slices remove one character each, not a header. They don't fix the length to a multiple of 100, and the windows don't overlap (stride = 100).

questions.question: Given the feature chunk 'hear me', what is the label chunk?
questions.answer: 'ear me' followed by the next character of the text, e.g. 'ear me ' if a space follows.
questions.explanation: Each label is the next character, so the label strip is the feature strip shifted by one.

questions.question: Why can the chunking be done on the raw string rather than after tokenization?
questions.answer: With a character-level tokenizer each character is one token, so a 100-character string always maps to a 100-integer sequence.
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. With word or subword tokenizers, string length and token count differ.

questions.question: If the corpus had exactly 1,000,001 characters, how many feature chunks would split_input produce, and how long is the last one?
questions.answer: shakespeare[:-1] has 1,000,000 characters, so there are 10,000 chunks, each exactly 100 characters long.
questions.explanation: range(0, 1,000,000, 100) gives 10,000 start indices. With 1,000,051 characters there would be 10,001 chunks and the last would have 50 characters, padded later by TextVectorization.

questions.question: How many next-character prediction targets does a single 100-character (x, y) pair provide?
questions.answer: 100, one per position.
questions.explanation: y is a full sequence, and the model predicts y[t] from x[0..t] at every t.

questions.question: In the printed sample, why does y[:50] end with a space while x[:50] ends with 'hear'?
questions.answer: Because y is shifted one character ahead: its 50th character is the one after 'hear' in the text, which is a space ('hear me speak').
questions.explanation: This confirms the offset-by-one alignment.

questions.question: Can you rewrite split_input so that consecutive chunks overlap by 50 characters? What would change in the dataset?
questions.answer: Use range(0, len(input), 50) with the same slice length; the number of chunks roughly doubles and each character appears in two chunks.
questions.explanation: This is an exercise beyond the book; it tests whether you understand the stride/window distinction.

questions.question: Which TextVectorization settings make the Shakespeare tokenizer character-level and preserve case and punctuation?
options: split='whitespace', standardize='lower_and_strip_punctuation'
split='character', standardize=None
split='character', standardize='lower'
output_mode='multi_hot', split=None
questions.answer: split='character', standardize=None
questions.explanation: Listing 15.3 uses exactly these. Whitespace splitting gives words; any standardization would alter case or punctuation; multi_hot produces bag-of-tokens vectors, not sequences.

questions.question: Why does generation benefit from skipping standardization, when classification in Chapter 14 used it?
questions.answer: A generator can only output tokens in its vocabulary. Removing case or punctuation would make the model unable to produce them, whereas a classifier's label does not depend on them.
questions.explanation: The page says case and punctuation are preserved and passed through unaltered.

questions.question: What shape does each batch from training_data have?
questions.answer: A pair of integer tensors (features, labels), each of shape (64, 100).
questions.explanation: Each sequence is padded or truncated to 100 IDs by output_sequence_length and batched in 64s.

questions.question: Why is an RNN described as the most natural fit for this language model?
questions.answer: Its recurrent state propagates information about past characters as it reads, so the prediction at each position depends only on the past, matching p(char | past chars).
questions.explanation: Stated on the page; the causal property is what p.452 shows a bidirectional GRU would violate.

questions.question: Why do the authors choose a GRU rather than an LSTM?
options: GRUs are bidirectional by default
It is fast and has a simpler internal state
LSTMs cannot process characters
GRUs do not need an Embedding layer
questions.answer: It is fast and has a simpler internal state
questions.explanation: The page says 'Any recurrent layer would do here', so LSTMs could process characters. GRUs are not bidirectional by default, and the Embedding is used either way.

questions.question: What happens to data ordering across epochs with dataset.shuffle(10_000).batch(64).cache(), and how would you change it?
questions.answer: The first epoch's shuffled batches are cached and replayed in the same order every epoch. Put cache() before shuffle(): dataset.cache().shuffle(10_000).batch(64).
questions.explanation: This is a tf.data detail, not discussed in the book; cache() stores whatever it receives during the first full iteration.

questions.question: Can you explain where the numbers 67, 256 and 100 on this page will appear in the model of Listing 15.4?
questions.answer: 67 is the Embedding input dimension and the Dense output width, 256 is the embedding dimension, and 100 is the input sequence length (shape (None, 100)).
questions.explanation: Check against the model summary on p.449.

questions.question: Verify the Embedding and Dense parameter counts.
questions.explanation: Embedding has one 256-d row per token and no bias; Dense has a weight per input-output pair plus one bias per output.

questions.question: Why is return_sequences=True needed?
options: To make the GRU bidirectional
To output a state at every step so a prediction can be made for every token
To reduce the number of parameters
To return the GRU's internal cell state for generation
questions.answer: To output a state at every step so a prediction can be made for every token
questions.explanation: Labels have shape (batch, 100). It does not add a backward pass, does not change parameter count, and returning the state is return_state (used on p.450).

questions.question: How many individual labels does one training batch contain, and why?
questions.answer: 6,400 = 64 samples x 100 characters, one next-character label per position.
questions.explanation: Stated on the page.

questions.question: In what sense is the language model 'still training on a classification problem'?
questions.answer: Each position is a 67-way classification of the next character with softmax and cross-entropy; there are just many of them per sequence.
questions.explanation: The authors' framing: one classification prediction for every token.

questions.question: What loss would a model that outputs a uniform distribution over the vocabulary get?
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy of the true class under a uniform 67-way distribution.

questions.question: Which layer holds most parameters?
options: Embedding
GRU
Dropout
Dense
questions.answer: GRU
questions.explanation: 3,938,304 of 4,024,131. Embedding (17,152) and Dense (68,675) are small because the vocabulary is only 67; Dropout has none.

questions.question: Can you derive the GRU's 3,938,304 parameters from embedding_dim and hidden_dim?
questions.explanation: Three blocks (update, reset, candidate), each with input kernel, recurrent kernel and two biases (Keras reset_after=True).

questions.question: Why can `generation_model.set_weights(model.get_weights())` succeed even though the two models have different input shapes?
options: Because Keras automatically resizes weights to the new input shape
Because no weight shape depends on sequence length, and the layers with weights appear in the same order with the same configurations
Because both models are trained jointly
Because the generation model has no trainable weights
questions.answer: Because no weight shape depends on sequence length, and the layers with weights appear in the same order with the same configurations
questions.explanation: Embedding, GRU and Dense weights depend only on vocabulary size, embedding_dim and hidden_dim. Keras does not resize weights; the generation model is not trained at all; and it does have weights, the copied ones.

questions.question: What two arguments in Listing 15.6 make the GRU's state explicit, and what does each do?
questions.answer: `return_state=True` makes the layer return its final state alongside its output; `initial_state=input_state` makes it start from the state passed in instead of zeros.
questions.explanation: Together they let the caller carry the memory from one call to the next.

questions.question: What would go wrong in generation if the GRU state were reset to zeros on each one-character call?
questions.answer: The model would see only the single current character with no context, so each prediction would be based on one character alone and the text would quickly become meaningless.
questions.explanation: The state contains all information encoded about past characters (p.450). Dropping it removes the conditioning on $x_{<t}$.

questions.question: What is an autoregressive model, as defined on this page?
options: A model whose output at one time step becomes its input at the next time step
A model that regresses continuous values
A model trained with automatic differentiation
A model that reads a sequence in both directions
questions.answer: A model whose output at one time step becomes its input at the next time step
questions.explanation: That is the page's definition. Regression of continuous values and autodiff are unrelated; bidirectional reading would actually break generation (p.452).

questions.question: Using the sizes from p.449 (vocabulary 67, embedding 256, hidden 1024), what are the output shapes of the two outputs of `generation_model` for a batch of 1?
questions.answer: Probabilities (1, 67) and state (1, 1024).
questions.explanation: Without `return_sequences` the GRU emits only its last output (1, 1024), which the Dense layer maps to (1, 67). The returned state has shape (1, hidden_dim).

questions.question: Why is Dropout missing from Listing 15.6, and does that change the predictions?
questions.answer: Dropout is only active during training and has no weights. At inference it is the identity, so leaving it out changes nothing.
questions.explanation: The training model applied Dropout(0.1) after the GRU (p.449). In `predict` it is disabled anyway.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why carrying the state makes each generation step cost the same regardless of how much text has already been generated?
questions.answer: The state is a fixed-size (1024) summary of all past input, so each step processes one token plus a constant-size vector.
questions.explanation: Without the state you would re-run the whole growing sequence at every step.

questions.question: In Listing 15.8, on the very first loop iteration, where does `predictions` come from?
options: It is initialized to zeros before the loop
It is the model's output after the last character of the prompt in Listing 15.7
It is computed by calling the training model on the prompt
It is a uniform distribution over the vocabulary
questions.answer: It is the model's output after the last character of the prompt in Listing 15.7
questions.explanation: The page says the final output prediction is saved to select the first generated character. Nothing initializes it to zeros or uniform values, and the training model is not used here.

questions.question: What shape is `inputs` in Listing 15.7, and why is `expand_dims` needed?
questions.answer: (1, 1). `[token_id]` has shape (1,), the per-sample shape the model expects; `expand_dims(axis=0)` adds the batch axis.
questions.explanation: The generation model's Input is `shape=(1,)` per sample (p.450), so with batch size 1 the tensor must be (1, 1).

questions.question: Why does feeding the prompt one token at a time give "the exact RNN state the model would see if this prompt had been encountered during training"?
questions.answer: Because the GRU is a recurrence that depends only on the previous state and the current input. Starting from the same zero state and carrying the state between calls performs exactly the same sequence of computations the layer performs internally over a full sequence.
questions.explanation: The weights are identical (set_weights on p.450) and the default initial state is zeros in both cases.

questions.question: How many calls to `generation_model.predict` happen in total across Listings 15.7 and 15.8 for the given prompt?
questions.explanation: The prompt "\nKING RICHARD III:\n" has 19 characters (a newline, the 17 characters of 'KING RICHARD III:' and a newline), one call each; the generation loop calls predict once per iteration for 250 iterations.

questions.question: Which decoding strategy does Listing 15.8 use?
options: Beam search
Random sampling with temperature
Greedy selection of the most likely character
Top-k sampling
questions.answer: Greedy selection of the most likely character
questions.explanation: `np.argmax(predictions, ...)` picks the highest-probability character. No beams, randomness or top-k truncation are involved; sampling strategies come up in chapter 16 (p.505).

questions.question: Why does the generation loop run for a fixed `max_length` instead of stopping when the model outputs a special token?
questions.answer: The model was trained on continuous 100-character chunks with no end-of-text token, so it never learned to signal the end. A fixed length is the simplest stopping rule.
questions.explanation: Contrast this with seq2seq decoding (p.453), which stops when "[end]" is generated.

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 15.8 to sample from `predictions` instead of taking the argmax? What would change about running it twice?
questions.answer: Replace the argmax with `np.random.choice(67, p=predictions[0])`. Two runs would then usually produce different text, whereas greedy decoding is deterministic.
questions.explanation: This previews the sampling discussion in chapter 16 (p.505).

questions.question: What happens, according to the page, if the GRU is replaced by `Bidirectional(GRU(...))`?
options: Training accuracy drops sharply and generation improves
Training accuracy rises above 99% immediately and generation stops working
Both training accuracy and generation improve
The model cannot be compiled
questions.answer: Training accuracy rises above 99% immediately and generation stops working
questions.explanation: The backward direction sees the next character, which is the label, so training becomes trivial. At generation time there is no future to read, so the model fails. The other options contradict the page.

questions.question: Explain the difference between the recurrent state loop and feeding predictions back. Which happens during training?
questions.answer: The state loop (h_t from h_{t-1} and x_t) happens in both training and inference. Feeding predicted labels back as the next input happens only at inference; training always uses the true previous characters.
questions.explanation: The page says: "at no point during training do we feed a model's predicted labels back into itself as input."

questions.question: Why can you not simply call `model.predict()` to generate text with a language model?
questions.answer: `predict` returns only next-token distributions for the inputs you give it. Generating requires a loop that picks a token, appends it, and calls the model again.
questions.explanation: The page calls this "an entire loop, and a nontrivial amount of logic, that exists only at inference time".

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT given on this page as a sequence-to-sequence problem?
options: Machine translation
Question answering
Translating a source text into a target-language sequence
Classifying a movie review as positive or negative
questions.answer: Classifying a movie review as positive or negative
questions.explanation: Classification maps a sequence to a single label, not to a sequence. Translation (which is what the third option describes) and question answering are both named on the page.

questions.question: Using the label construction from p.447, explain precisely why a backward-running GRU makes the task 'trivially easy'.
questions.answer: The label at position t is the input at t+1. A backward GRU's output at position t has already processed input t+1, so it can output that character directly.
questions.explanation: This is target leakage: the answer is part of the input.

questions.question: What features of Shakespeare's text has the model clearly learned, judging from the sample?
questions.answer: Uppercase speaker names followed by a colon and newline, real character names, archaic words (thou, hath, wouldst), punctuation and verse-like line lengths.
questions.explanation: Meaning across lines is weak, consistent with a small character-level model trained briefly.

questions.question: Can you predict what you would see if a Transformer language model were trained without hiding future tokens? Relate it to the Bidirectional GRU warning.
questions.answer: The same thing: near-perfect training accuracy and failed generation, because each position could attend to the next token, which is the label.
questions.explanation: The decoder block in section 15.3.3 (p.470) must keep future positions hidden for this reason.

questions.question: In figure 15.1's training phase, what is the decoder's target output?
options: [start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy
qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]
how, is, the, weather, today
[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]
questions.answer: qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]
questions.explanation: The decoder predicts the target offset by one step. The first option is the decoder's input, the third is the encoder's input, and the fourth is neither.

questions.question: What are the roles of "[start]" and "[end]" in seq2seq inference?
questions.answer: [start] is the seed token given to the decoder to predict the first real token; [end] is the stop token whose generation ends the loop.
questions.explanation: Both are described in the inference bullets on the page.

questions.question: In what sense is the seq2seq decoder 'trained using the language modeling setup we saw previously'? What is different?
questions.answer: Like the Shakespeare model, it predicts the next token from all previous (true) tokens, with labels shifted by one. The difference is that it also conditions on the encoder's representation of a separate source sequence.
questions.explanation: The italicized *and* on the page stresses the two sources of information.

questions.question: Which component may legitimately read its input in both directions?
options: Only the decoder
Only the encoder
Both encoder and decoder
Neither
questions.answer: Only the encoder
questions.explanation: The source is fully known, so the encoder can be bidirectional (p.458). The decoder is a language model, and future target tokens would leak the label (p.452, p.458).

questions.question: Why can the seq2seq generation loop stop by itself while the Shakespeare loop ran for a fixed 250 steps?
questions.answer: Every training target ends with [end], so the decoder learns to predict it when the output is complete. The Shakespeare model was trained on continuous chunks with no end marker.
questions.explanation: The stop token is part of the training labels.

questions.question: For the figure's example, how many next-token predictions does the decoder make per training example, and how many inference loop iterations are needed if every prediction is correct?
questions.answer: 5 predictions in training (qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]); 5 inference iterations, the last producing [end].
questions.explanation: The decoder input has 5 tokens and so does the shifted label sequence.

questions.question: Without looking at the figure, can you write the decoder input and labels for translating 'I am hungry' to 'tengo hambre'?
questions.answer: Decoder input: [start] tengo hambre. Labels: tengo hambre [end]. Encoder input: I am hungry.
questions.explanation: Apply the one-step offset with the special tokens.

questions.question: Why are [start] and [end] added only to the Spanish sentences?
options: Spanish has more punctuation
Spanish is the target sequence the decoder generates
The English tokenizer cannot handle brackets
To make the sentences equal in length
questions.answer: Spanish is the target sequence the decoder generates
questions.explanation: The decoder needs a seed token and a stop token (Figure 15.1). Punctuation, bracket handling and length equalization are not the reason.

questions.question: With 20,000 pairs, how many go to training, validation and test?
questions.answer: val = test = 3,000; train = 14,000.

questions.question: What does [:-1] do in `f.read().split("\n")[:-1]`?
questions.answer: Drops the empty string that follows the file's final newline.
questions.explanation: Splitting 'a\nb\n' on newlines gives ['a', 'b', ''].

questions.question: Why must the shuffle precede the slicing?
questions.answer: Slices are contiguous; without shuffling, each split would inherit the file's ordering and not be a random sample.
questions.explanation: Representative splits require random assignment.

questions.question: Why are spaces included in "[start] " and " [end]"?
questions.answer: So that the markers become separate tokens when the text is split on whitespace.
questions.explanation: Otherwise '[start]¿quién' would be one token.

questions.question: Could you explain how the [start] token will be used at inference time?
questions.answer: The decoder receives [start] plus the encoded source, predicts the first word, feeds it back, and loops until [end].
questions.explanation: Described with Figure 15.1 on p.453.

questions.question: Why are [ and ] removed from strip_chars?
options: They are not punctuation
So [start] and [end] remain distinct from the words start and end
Because re.escape cannot handle them
Because Spanish does not use brackets
questions.answer: So [start] and [end] remain distinct from the words start and end
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. They are in string.punctuation, re.escape handles them fine, and Spanish usage of brackets is irrelevant.

questions.question: Why is the Spanish output_sequence_length sequence_length + 1?
questions.answer: So the 21 tokens can be split into a 20-token decoder input and a 20-token target offset by one step.
questions.explanation: Target is 'the Spanish sentence offset by one step ahead'.

questions.question: What are sample_weights used for in this pipeline?
questions.answer: To tell Keras which label positions count in loss and metrics, ignoring zero-padded positions.
questions.explanation: Targets have different lengths and are padded with zeros (p.456).

questions.question: Which standardization does the English tokenizer use?
options: custom_standardization
None
The default (lowercase and strip punctuation)
Character splitting
questions.answer: The default (lowercase and strip punctuation)
questions.explanation: No standardize argument is passed, so Keras's default applies. custom_standardization is only for Spanish; None and character splitting were used for Shakespeare (p.448).

questions.question: Why adapt the tokenizers on train_english_texts / train_spanish_texts rather than all pairs?
questions.answer: To avoid leaking validation/test information into the vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Standard practice: preprocessing state is learned from training data only.

questions.question: What would a production translator do differently with punctuation, and why?
questions.answer: Keep punctuation characters as separate tokens so it can generate correctly punctuated output.
questions.explanation: Stated in the note after the bullets.

questions.question: Can you predict what custom_standardization returns for '[start] ¡Hola! [end]'?
questions.answer: '[start] ¡hola [end]': the ! is removed but ¡ is not in strip_chars.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of string.punctuation and the listing's limitation.

questions.question: Why does the Spanish `TextVectorization` layer output `sequence_length + 1` tokens?
options: To leave room for the `[UNK]` token
So that after dropping one token for the decoder input and one for the labels, both have length `sequence_length`
Because Spanish sentences are on average longer than English ones
Because the Bidirectional encoder doubles the sequence length
questions.answer: So that after dropping one token for the decoder input and one for the labels, both have length `sequence_length`
questions.explanation: `spa[:, :-1]` and `spa[:, 1:]` each remove one position from a 21-token tensor, giving 20 tokens each, which matches the printed shapes `(64, 20)`. `[UNK]` takes a vocabulary slot, not a sequence slot. Sentence-length statistics have nothing to do with it. The encoder (p.458) returns a single vector and does not change sequence length.

questions.question: What does `sample_weights = labels != 0` compute, and what would go wrong without it?
questions.answer: A boolean (64, 20) mask that is True for real target tokens and False for padding. Without it, the loss and accuracy would include many trivially predictable padding positions, inflating accuracy and wasting gradient signal.
questions.explanation: The page says translations vary in length and some label sequences are padded with zeros, and that only predictions for non-zero labels matter.

questions.question: Labels for one sentence are `[45, 17, 803, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0]` and the model predicts `[45, 17, 9, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0]`. Compute the unweighted and the sample-weighted accuracy.
questions.answer: Unweighted: 7/8 = 87.5%. Weighted: 3/4 = 75%.
questions.explanation: The weights are `[1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0]`. Among the 4 real tokens, 3 are correct (token 803 was mispredicted as 9). Unweighted accuracy also counts the 4 padding positions, which are all correct.

questions.question: The English tokens are not shifted, but the Spanish tokens are. Why the asymmetry?
questions.answer: English is the fixed conditioning input (encoder input) that the model never predicts, so the whole sentence is given. Spanish is generated token by token, so it is set up as a language model: the inputs are the previous tokens and the labels are the next tokens.
questions.explanation: The page describes this as the off-by-one setup of the generation model 'with the addition of the fixed encoder inputs, which will be handled separately'.

questions.question: In `make_dataset`, what is the main benefit of calling `batch()` before `map(format_dataset)`?
options: It makes the labels shorter
The tokenizers process 64 strings per call, which is vectorized and faster
It is required for `cache()` to work
It guarantees each epoch sees a new shuffle
questions.answer: The tokenizers process 64 strings per call, which is vectorized and faster
questions.explanation: Batching first means `format_dataset` receives a batch of strings, so `TextVectorization` runs on 64 strings at once. Label length is fixed by the tokenizer. `cache()` works in any position. Per-epoch reshuffling depends on where `cache()` sits, not on batching.

questions.question: Why does the naive approach introduced at the end of the page (one RNN emitting a target token at each source time step) look problematic even before reading p.457?
questions.answer: When it emits target token N it has read only source tokens 0...N, so it cannot use later source words. Languages with different word order need information from the end of the source to produce the start of the target.
questions.explanation: This anticipates the argument on p.457 ("Te traeré la bolsa" starts with the translation of "you", the last English word). That is why an encoder first reads the whole source.

questions.question: Without looking, write down the three components returned by `format_dataset` and their shapes for one batch.
questions.answer: features = {"english": (64, 20), "spanish": (64, 20)}; labels = (64, 20); sample_weights = (64, 20) boolean.
questions.explanation: Compare with the interactive output on the page. If you wrote 21 anywhere, revisit the off-by-one slicing.

questions.question: Why can't the naive `LSTM(return_sequences=True)` model correctly produce "Te" as the first word of "Te traeré la bolsa"?
options: The LSTM has too few units (32)
At the first output step the model has only seen the first English word, but "Te" corresponds to the last English word, "you"
The Dense layer cannot output Spanish tokens
The Embedding dimension of 128 is too small to represent pronouns
questions.answer: At the first output step the model has only seen the first English word, but "Te" corresponds to the last English word, "you"
questions.explanation: The page's argument is about step-by-step causality, not capacity. Unit count and embedding size affect capacity but cannot supply unseen information. The Dense layer outputs a distribution over the target vocabulary and can output any token.

questions.question: In figure 15.2, what exactly flows from the encoder RNN to the decoder RNN?
questions.answer: A single representation of the whole source: the encoder's final output vector or its final internal state, used as the decoder's initial state.
questions.explanation: The figure labels the connection 'Final output vector, or final internal state' and marks it as 'Initial state' on the decoder.

questions.question: How does the decoder of figure 15.2 differ from the Shakespeare generator of section 15.1?
questions.answer: Both are next-token language models. The Shakespeare generator starts from an initial state of zeros, while the seq2seq decoder starts from the encoder's representation of the English sentence, so its predictions are conditioned on the source.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly: 'instead of an initial state of zeros, which we used in our Shakespeare generator'.

questions.question: Why is it fine for the encoder to pass information from the end of the source to its beginning, but not fine for the decoder to do the same with the target?
questions.answer: The encoder makes no predictions, so there is nothing to leak. The decoder predicts each next target token, so seeing future target tokens would reveal the answers and make the loss trivial.
questions.explanation: The page explains the encoder side; p.458 makes the decoder side explicit with its warning about a Bidirectional decoder.

questions.question: In figure 15.2, what is the decoder's input sequence when its output is "qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]"?
options: how, is, the, weather, today
[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy
qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]
[start], how, is, the, weather
questions.answer: [start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy
questions.explanation: The decoder input is its output shifted right with `[start]` in front, the off-by-one setup from p.456. The English tokens go into the encoder, not the decoder. Feeding the output itself would leak the answer.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters of the naive model on this page with vocab_size = 15,000 (Embedding 128, LSTM 32, Dense softmax).
questions.explanation: An LSTM has 4 gates, each with input weights (128×32), recurrent weights (32×32) and a bias (32). A Dense layer has in×out weights plus out biases. (The book does not print this summary; it is a worked exercise.)

questions.question: Explain, in two sentences, the 'single representation' weakness of the encoder-decoder RNN and predict what problem it causes for long sentences.
questions.answer: Everything about the source must be packed into one fixed-size state vector, whatever the sentence length. Long or complex sentences lose information, which p.461 names as a fundamental limitation.
questions.explanation: Check your answer against the first bullet on p.461.

questions.question: Why does the encoder use `merge_mode="sum"` in its Bidirectional wrapper?
options: Summing is more accurate than concatenation for all tasks
It keeps the output at 1,024 dimensions so it can serve as the initial state of the 1,024-unit decoder GRU
It halves the number of encoder parameters
It makes the encoder causal
questions.answer: It keeps the output at 1,024 dimensions so it can serve as the initial state of the 1,024-unit decoder GRU
questions.explanation: Concatenation would give 2,048 dimensions, which does not match the decoder's state size. Merge mode does not change parameter count (both directions still have their own weights, 7,876,608 total on p.459). Summing does not make anything causal. No merge mode is universally more accurate.

questions.question: The authors say a Bidirectional decoder 'would break training by making the loss function trivially easy'. Explain the mechanism.
questions.answer: The decoder's target at position t is its input at position t+1. A backward RNN carries information from later positions to earlier ones, so position t would 'see' its own label and the model could copy it rather than learn to translate.
questions.explanation: This follows from the off-by-one setup on p.456 and the causal requirement stated on this page.

questions.question: Verify the 3,840,000 parameters reported for `embedding_1`, and predict the parameter count of the Spanish embedding.
questions.answer: 15,000 × 256 = 3,840,000. The Spanish embedding has the same vocab size and dimension, so it also has 3,840,000 (confirmed as embedding_2 on p.459).
questions.explanation: An Embedding layer stores one embed_dim vector per vocabulary entry and has no bias.

questions.question: What is the `not_equal (NotEqual)` row in the summary, and where does its output go?
questions.answer: It computes the padding mask `english != 0` created by `mask_zero=True`. The mask is fed to the Bidirectional GRU so that padding is skipped.
questions.explanation: On p.459 the bidirectional row lists `embedding_1[0][0], not_equal[0][0]` under 'Connected to'.

questions.question: Which single line connects the English sentence's information to the Spanish decoder?
options: `x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)`
`x = rnn_layer(x, initial_state=encoder_output)`
`seq2seq_rnn = keras.Model([source, target], target_predictions)`
`target = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="spanish")`
questions.answer: `x = rnn_layer(x, initial_state=encoder_output)`
questions.explanation: The encoder output enters the decoder only as its initial state. Dropout is regularization. `keras.Model` just declares inputs and outputs. The Spanish Input carries only Spanish tokens.

questions.question: Why are both inputs declared with `shape=(None,)` even though the dataset always produces 20-token sequences?
questions.answer: So the model accepts sequences of any length, such as variable-length inputs at inference or different source and target lengths. Training happens to use 20.
questions.explanation: The summary shows `(None, None)` for both inputs: unknown batch and time dimensions.

questions.question: Sketch the model graph from memory: inputs, embeddings, mask, encoder, decoder, dropout, output. Then check it against the summary on pp.458-459.
questions.answer: english → Embedding(+mask) → Bidirectional GRU(1024, sum) → [initial state] → GRU(1024, seq) ← Embedding ← spanish; GRU → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(15000, softmax).
questions.explanation: If you drew an arrow from the English embedding straight to the decoder at every step, revisit p.457: the source enters only through the initial state.

questions.question: Which layer contributes the most parameters to `seq2seq_rnn`?
options: The Bidirectional GRU encoder
The decoder GRU
The output Dense layer
The English Embedding layer
questions.answer: The output Dense layer
questions.explanation: The Dense layer has 15,375,000 parameters, compared with 7,876,608 for the Bidirectional GRU, 3,938,304 for the decoder GRU and 3,840,000 for each embedding. Its size comes from the 15,000-token vocabulary times the 1,024-d input.

questions.question: Show that the Bidirectional encoder's 7,876,608 parameters are exactly twice the decoder GRU's count, using GRU units 1,024 and input dimension 256.
questions.explanation: Keras GRUs have, per gate group, an input kernel, a recurrent kernel and two bias vectors (reset_after=True). The decoder GRU also takes 256-d embeddings, so its count matches one direction.

questions.question: According to the authors, why is next-token accuracy not a great metric for machine translation?
questions.answer: It assumes the correct target tokens 0 to N are known when predicting token N + 1. At inference the model generates from scratch, and its previous tokens may be wrong, so the metric does not reflect real generation quality.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in e06. BLEU against reference translations is offered as a better, standard alternative.

questions.question: Why does the compile call use `weighted_metrics=["accuracy"]` rather than `metrics=["accuracy"]`?
questions.answer: The dataset provides sample weights that zero out padding positions, and only weighted metrics use them. Plain metrics would count padding predictions and inflate accuracy.
questions.explanation: See `sample_weights = labels != 0` on p.456.

questions.question: What property of BLEU does the book highlight?
options: It is differentiable and can be used as a training loss
It measures similarity to high-quality reference translations and tolerates slightly misaligned sequences
It counts only exact sentence matches
It requires no reference translations
questions.answer: It measures similarity to high-quality reference translations and tolerates slightly misaligned sequences
questions.explanation: This paraphrases the page. BLEU is not differentiable in its standard form, it rewards partial (n-gram) matches rather than only exact sentences, and it needs references.

questions.question: Verify that 34,869,912 float32 parameters occupy about 133.02 MB as printed.
questions.explanation: Keras reports sizes in binary megabytes. Each float32 weight is 4 bytes.

questions.question: Describe the inference loop in your own words: what goes into the decoder at the first step, what happens to each prediction, and when does it stop?
questions.answer: First step: the `[start]` token plus the encoded English sentence. Each predicted token is appended to the decoded sequence and fed back in. The loop stops at `[end]` or at the maximum sentence length.
questions.explanation: Compare with e07 and Listing 15.13 on p.460.

questions.question: In Listing 15.13, why is the prediction taken from `next_token_predictions[0, i, :]`?
options: Position i is the last real token of the current prefix, and its output was trained to predict the following token
Position i always contains the [end] token
The model only outputs i positions at step i
Index i selects the i-th example in the batch
questions.answer: Position i is the last real token of the current prefix, and its output was trained to predict the following token
questions.explanation: After i iterations the prefix has i+1 tokens (indices 0…i). Targets were offset by one in training, so the output at index i predicts token i+1. [end] is not at position i. The model always outputs 21 positions because of padding. The batch index is the first axis (0), not i.

questions.question: The variable is called `sampled_token_index`. Is the token actually sampled? What would change if it were?
questions.answer: No. `np.argmax` picks the most likely token deterministically (greedy decoding). Sampling would draw from the softmax distribution (e.g. `np.random.choice(15000, p=probs)`), so repeated calls could give different translations, and sometimes worse ones.
questions.explanation: Greedy decoding has no randomness. Sampling, as used for text generation elsewhere in the book, adds diversity, which is rarely wanted in translation.

questions.question: Give the two sources of run-to-run variation that the authors name for the translations.
questions.answer: The random initialization of the weights and the random shuffling of the input data during training.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph after the listing (e05).

questions.question: Suppose a translation ends after 8 decoding steps. With Listing 15.13, how many decoder positions are processed in total, given that the Spanish input is always padded to 21 tokens? How many would a cached RNN decoder process?
questions.answer: 8 × 21 = 168 decoder positions (plus 8 × 20 = 160 encoder positions). A cached decoder needs 8 positions (plus one 20-step encoding).
questions.explanation: Each `predict` call reprocesses the full padded target and source. Caching the GRU state lets each step process only the new token (p.461).

questions.question: Which error type does the output "te lo voy mañana a decir" for "I will tell you tomorrow." illustrate?
options: Word-order error
Out-of-vocabulary token
Hallucinated content
Premature [end] token
questions.answer: Word-order error
questions.explanation: All words of the correct translation *te lo voy a decir mañana* are present, but *mañana* sits inside the periphrasis *voy a decir*. There is no [UNK] here, nothing is invented, and the sentence is complete.

questions.question: Why does the model output contain no capital letters or punctuation even though the English input does?
questions.answer: The Spanish tokenizer was built with `custom_standardization`, which lowercases text and strips punctuation (including ¿) except the square brackets. The model therefore only knows lowercase, unpunctuated tokens.
questions.explanation: See Listing 15.9 on p.455. The authors note that a non-toy model would keep punctuation as tokens.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write the generation loop yourself, including where to read the prediction and when to stop?
questions.answer: Self-check: tokenize the source once; prefix='[start]'; loop up to 20 times: tokenize prefix, predict, argmax at index i, look up the word, append, break on '[end]'.
questions.explanation: If you could not place index `i` correctly, revisit the offset-by-one targets (p.456).

questions.question: According to the book, what does the decoder really need to predict a new token in an efficient RNN inference loop?
options: The current token and the previous RNN state
The entire source sentence and the entire generated target
Only the encoder's final state
All previous predicted probability distributions
questions.answer: The current token and the previous RNN state
questions.explanation: The RNN state summarizes all earlier tokens, so only the newest token and the cached state are needed. Reprocessing everything (option 2) is what the inefficient loop does. The encoder state alone ignores the generated prefix. Previous distributions are not inputs to the model.

questions.question: Name the two fundamental limitations of the RNN approach to seq2seq listed on this page.
questions.answer: (1) The source representation must be held entirely in the encoder state vector, which limits sentence size and complexity. (2) RNNs progressively forget the past on long sequences, so little remains about the start by the 100th token.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets on p.461.

questions.question: Why would a larger encoder state (say 4,096 instead of 1,024 units) not fundamentally solve the first limitation?
questions.answer: The capacity is still fixed while source sentences can be arbitrarily long, and the decoder still cannot selectively look up specific source tokens. Attention instead gives access to one vector per source token, so memory grows with the input.
questions.explanation: The problem is structural (a single fixed channel), not just a matter of size.

questions.question: What was surprising about 'Attention Is All You Need' at the time, according to the authors?
options: That attention could be the only mechanism used to pass information across a sequence
That attention could be used in NLP at all
That LSTMs could be stacked seven layers deep
That translation could be done with neural networks
questions.answer: That attention could be the only mechanism used to pass information across a sequence
questions.explanation: The book says attention 'was not new' and had been used in NLP for a couple of years. The novelty was dropping recurrence entirely. Deep LSTM stacks and neural translation already existed.

questions.question: Explain in terms of path length why RNNs forget the start of long sequences while attention does not.
questions.answer: In an RNN, information from token 1 reaches token 100 only through 99 sequential state updates, each of which can overwrite it, and gradients shrink along that path. Attention connects any two positions directly in one step through a weighted sum.
questions.explanation: Path length O(N) vs O(1) between positions. This is additional explanation building on the second bullet.

questions.question: Can you sketch how you would restructure Listing 15.13 to cache the RNN state?
questions.answer: Self-check: encode once; loop feeding only the last token plus the cached GRU state into a one-step decoder that returns the new state; argmax; stop on [end].
questions.explanation: If unsure, review how GRU states are passed as `initial_state` on p.458.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the fundamental reason RNNs struggle to recall information from early in a long sequence?
options: They have too few parameters to store long sequences.
They lack any mechanism to refer back to a previous part of the sequence directly; all information must pass through the cell state at every position.
They cannot process sequences longer than 100,000 tokens.
They use convolutions that only see a local window.
questions.answer: They lack any mechanism to refer back to a previous part of the sequence directly; all information must pass through the cell state at every position.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the second printed paragraph. Parameter count is not the argument; 100,000 is the word count of the book in the analogy, not an RNN limit; and RNNs are not convolutional.

questions.question: Which two adjectives do the authors use for the way humans pull information from text?
questions.answer: Selective and contextual.
questions.explanation: Humans use only some of the text (selective), and which part depends on the current task (contextual). Attention is designed to provide both.

questions.question: Map the book-reading thought experiment onto an RNN and onto attention. What does "closing the book" correspond to?
questions.answer: Closing the book corresponds to an RNN keeping only its final internal state and working from that summary. Attention corresponds to keeping the book open and flipping to the relevant chapter or listing, with the current task deciding where to look.
questions.explanation: The authors make this comparison explicitly: an RNN must carry everything through its state, like implementing the model from memory after closing the book.

questions.question: In figure 15.3, what does the attention-score image show?
options: A blurred copy of the cat produced by a convolution.
A per-location map of how much each part of the input should matter, bright over the cat's face.
The gradient of the loss with respect to the pixels.
A random mask used for dropout.
questions.answer: A per-location map of how much each part of the input should matter, bright over the cat's face.
questions.explanation: The caption says input features are assigned attention scores that inform the next representation; the new representation keeps the face and darkens the background. It is not a convolution output, a gradient, or a dropout mask.

questions.question: Why is the word "contextually" essential in the authors' definition of attention?
questions.answer: Because the weights given to the parts of the sequence depend on the current input being processed. The same source sentence is weighted differently when predicting different target words.
questions.explanation: A fixed weighting would just be another static layer. Attention recomputes relevance for each current input, which is what lets it act like targeted lookup.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, why a question-answering RNN would get worse as the source document grows, and what attention changes?
questions.answer: The RNN must compress the whole document into a fixed-size state before seeing what is needed, and early content fades over many updates. Attention keeps every position available and retrieves the relevant ones, weighted by relevance to the current input.
questions.explanation: If you can state both halves, the bottleneck and the direct weighted lookup, you are ready for dot-product attention on p.463-464.

questions.question: Which operation does np.einsum("ijk,ijk->", x, y) perform?
options: Element-wise multiplication returning an array of shape (i, j, k)
Element-wise multiplication followed by summing everything into a scalar
A transpose of x
A batched matrix multiplication
questions.answer: Element-wise multiplication followed by summing everything into a scalar
questions.explanation: All letters are repeated (multiplied) and none appear in the output (all summed). "ijk,ijk->ijk" would keep the shape; a transpose has one input; a batched matmul needs a contracted inner axis with other axes kept.

questions.question: Write the formula computed by np.einsum("hij,jk->hik", A, B), and give the output shape if A has shape (8, 3, 4) and B has shape (4, 5).
questions.answer: $C_{hik} = \sum_j A_{hij}B_{jk}$, shape (8, 3, 5).
questions.explanation: j is shared and dropped, so it is summed; h, i and k are kept in that order. Each of the 8 matrices of shape (3, 4) is multiplied by the (4, 5) matrix.

questions.question: What are the two ways to use einsum in Keras mentioned in the sidebar?
questions.answer: keras.ops.einsum, a drop-in replacement for np.einsum, and keras.layers.EinsumDense, a Dense layer where the matmul is replaced by an einsum.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last sentence of the sidebar.

questions.question: Why does "ijk,ijk->ijk" not sum anything even though every letter is repeated?
questions.answer: Summation applies only to letters missing from the output. All three letters appear in the output, so the values are only multiplied element-wise.
questions.explanation: Rule 1 (multiply repeated letters) and rule 2 (sum letters absent from the output) are separate.

questions.question: In the setup of section 15.3.1, what does the attention score function take as input?
options: Two source vectors
The target vector being predicted and one source vector
The final GRU state only
The whole target sequence and the loss
questions.answer: The target vector being predicted and one source vector
questions.explanation: The page writes score(target_vector, source_vector) and applies it to every source vector. Comparing source vectors with each other is self-attention (p.468); the final state alone was the RNN bottleneck; the loss plays no role in scoring.

questions.question: Using einsum rules, what shape does np.einsum("btd,bsd->bts", target, source) produce for target of shape (32, 10, 64) and source of shape (32, 12, 64)?
questions.explanation: b and d are shared; d is dropped and summed (a dot product over 64 features); b, t and s remain. This is the score matrix used on p.464.

questions.question: Can you write einsum strings for: a matrix-vector product, a batched dot product of two (batch, d) arrays, and an outer product of two vectors?
questions.answer: "ij,j->i", "bd,bd->b", "i,j->ij".
questions.explanation: If these came easily, the attention einsums on the next pages will read naturally. The outer product shows that letters need not be shared: nothing is summed, and every pair is multiplied.

questions.question: Why do the authors pass the attention scores through softmax?
options: To make the scores sparse so only one source word is used
So that the scores for a given target sum to 1, giving the weighted sum a predictable magnitude
To add learnable parameters to the score
To make the computation run in a loop over the source
questions.answer: So that the scores for a given target sum to 1, giving the weighted sum a predictable magnitude
questions.explanation: This is the reason stated in the first paragraph. Softmax is not sparse (all weights are positive), it has no parameters, and it does not introduce loops.

questions.question: Two source vectors $s_1 = (1, 0)$ and $s_2 = (0, 2)$, target $t = (1, 1)$. Compute the dot-product scores, the softmax weights and the combined vector.
questions.answer: Scores 1 and 2; weights $e/(e+e^2) \approx 0.27$ and $e^2/(e+e^2) \approx 0.73$; combined $\approx 0.27\cdot(1,0) + 0.73\cdot(0,2) = (0.27, 1.46)$.
questions.explanation: Follow the three lines of the pseudocode: score, softmax, weighted sum.

questions.question: What do the letters b, t, s and d stand for in np.einsum("btd,bsd->bts", target, source)?
questions.answer: Batch size, target length, source length and vector size.
questions.explanation: Given in the code callout. d is summed over, so the result has shape (b, t, s).

questions.question: In figure 15.4, why might "traeré" attend mostly to "I" and "bring"?
questions.answer: "Traeré" means "I will bring": it encodes the subject and the verb, so those source words carry the information needed to produce it.
questions.explanation: The figure shows the darkest arrows to "I" and "bring", illustrating that relevance depends on what is being predicted.

questions.question: What does each row of the attention score matrix represent?
options: How much one source word is used by all target words
How much a target word values each source word in the weighted sum
The embedding of one source word
The gradient for one target word
questions.answer: How much a target word values each source word in the weighted sum
questions.explanation: The text says so directly; softmax over axis=-1 normalizes each such row. Columns, not rows, correspond to source words.

questions.question: Why is the dot product a reasonable relevance score, and what assumption does it encode?
questions.answer: It is large when the target and source vectors point in similar directions. The assumption is that a source token whose vector is close to the target vector is relevant to the prediction, so the model must learn representations where this holds.
questions.explanation: The authors say they will examine why this assumption makes intuitive sense at the end of the chapter. It is also cheap: a single matrix product.

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, the three lines of the single-target pseudocode and the two lines of the vectorized version on this page?
questions.answer: scores = [score(target, source) for source in sources]; scores = softmax(scores); combined = np.sum(scores * sources). Vectorized: scores = np.einsum("btd,bsd->bts", target, source); scores = softmax(scores, axis=-1).
questions.explanation: These lines, plus the return on p.465, are the full dot-product attention.

questions.question: In np.einsum("bts,bsd->btd", scores, source), which axis is summed over?
options: b (batch)
t (target)
s (source)
d (vector size)
questions.answer: s (source)
questions.explanation: s appears in both inputs but not in the output, so it is multiplied and summed: a weighted sum over source positions. b, t and d all survive in btd.

questions.question: In the photo-search analogy, what are the query, the keys and the values?
questions.answer: The query is the search term, the keys are the photo tags matched against the query, and the values are the photos themselves.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph on terminology (and drawn in figure 15.6).

questions.question: Why does projecting the target and source vectors with Dense layers make attention more expressive?
questions.answer: Without projections, the score can only use whatever similarity already exists between the raw vectors. With learned projections, the model can find a shared space where source vectors that help prediction are close to the target, learning what "relevant" means.
questions.explanation: The book calls this making the hypothesis space richer.

questions.question: Why is the three-argument form sum(score(query, key) * value) more general than sum(score(target, source) * source)?
options: It allows the vector used for scoring to differ from the vector that is summed
It removes the need for softmax
It makes attention run over a loop
It allows several targets to share one score
questions.answer: It allows the vector used for scoring to differ from the vector that is summed
questions.explanation: The book says in rare cases you might not want to use the same vector to score as to sum. Softmax is still used, there are no loops, and per-target scores remain.

questions.question: In figure 15.5, which English word does the row for "la" attend to most, and why does that make sense?
questions.answer: "the": "la" is the Spanish feminine article that translates "the".
questions.explanation: The cell ("la", "the") is the darkest in that row. Similarly "bolsa" attends most to "bag".

questions.question: If scores has shape (16, 9, 12) and source has shape (16, 12, 128), what shape does the return line produce, and what does each output vector represent?
questions.answer: (16, 9, 128): for each of 16 examples and each of 9 target positions, a 128-d weighted sum of the 12 source vectors.
questions.explanation: s = 12 is summed out; b, t and d remain.

questions.question: Can you name the role of each of the four Dense layers created at the bottom of the page?
questions.answer: query_dense projects the target for scoring; key_dense projects the source for scoring; value_dense projects the source before it is combined; output_dense projects the result after the summation.
questions.explanation: These map directly onto the sentence "project the source vectors into an entirely separate space before they are combined and once again after the summation".

questions.question: In `np.einsum("btd,bsd->bts", query, key)`, which axis is summed over?
options: d, the feature axis
s, the source axis
t, the target axis
b, the batch axis
questions.answer: d, the feature axis
questions.explanation: d appears in both inputs but not in the output, so it is multiplied and summed, which is a dot product. b, t and s all appear in the output. s is summed only in the second einsum.

questions.question: Query and key components are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1, and d = 64. What is the standard deviation of a raw dot-product score, and what is the scaling factor?
questions.answer: Var = 64, so std = 8. The scores are divided by √64 = 8, giving std ≈ 1.
questions.explanation: A sum of d unit-variance products has variance d. Dividing by √d normalizes it.

questions.question: Why do very large dot-product scores hurt training?
questions.answer: Large scores make the softmax nearly one-hot. Its Jacobian diag(p) − ppᵀ then approaches zero, so almost no gradient flows back to the queries and keys, and training becomes unstable or stalls.
questions.explanation: The book says large scores 'can affect the stability of our softmax gradients'. This answer spells out the mechanism.

questions.question: In figure 15.6, what plays the role of the query, the keys and the values?
questions.answer: Query: the search text "dogs on the beach". Keys: the tags of each photo. Values: the photos themselves.
questions.explanation: Stated in the caption and on p.465.

questions.question: What is the output shape of `parameterized_attention(query=target, key=source, value=source)` for a target of length 12 and a source of length 20 (ignoring feature size)?
options: (batch, 12, features)
(batch, 20, features)
questions.answer: (batch, 12, features)
questions.explanation: There is one output vector per query (target) position. (batch, 12, 20) is the score matrix, not the output. A source-length output would need source queries.

questions.question: What does 'washed out' mean in the context of the second refinement, and why does a single softmax sum cause it?
questions.answer: When a target position spreads its weight over many source tokens, the output is an average of their value vectors, and distinctive features of each token get diluted. A single softmax produces only one such average per position, so it cannot keep several separate pieces of information sharp.
questions.explanation: This motivates running several attention heads with separate parameters (p.467).

questions.question: Can you write `parameterized_attention` from memory, including the √d scaling, and give each intermediate shape?
questions.answer: Self-check against the illustrative code: (b,t,d) and (b,s,d) → scores (b,t,s) → weights (b,t,s) → output (b,t,d) → projected output.
questions.explanation: If the einsums are unclear, revisit p.463.

questions.question: How are the outputs of the different heads combined in multi-head attention?
options: Concatenated along the feature axis, then passed through a Dense layer
Averaged element-wise
Summed and then softmax-normalized
Only the head with the highest score is kept
questions.answer: Concatenated along the feature axis, then passed through a Dense layer
questions.explanation: `ops.concatenate(head_outputs, axis=-1)` followed by `output_dense`. Averaging or summing would bring back the washing-out problem, and nothing selects a single head.

questions.question: What problem do multiple heads solve, in the book's words?
questions.answer: When attending to too many tokens at once, the interesting features of individual source tokens get 'washed out' in the combined representation. Multiple heads avoid having to combine the entire source sequence with a single softmax sum.
questions.explanation: From e03 and e05.

questions.question: Find the bug on the `scores = np.einsum(...)` line of the printed pseudocode and explain its consequence.
questions.answer: It uses `target` and `source` instead of the projected `query` and `key` (and the weighted sum uses `source` instead of `value`). The learned projections are therefore never used, and every head computes the same unparameterized attention, so multiple heads would be pointless.
questions.explanation: The text says heads run 'the same computation with different parameters'. That only holds if the projected tensors are used.

questions.question: With hidden size 256 split over 8 heads, what is head_dim, what is the scaling divisor, and what is the concatenated output width?
questions.answer: head_dim = 32; divisor = √32 ≈ 5.66; concatenated width = 8 × 32 = 256.
questions.explanation: Matches `key_dim = hidden_dim // num_heads` in Listing 15.14 (p.469) and the model in Listing 15.16 (p.473).

questions.question: Why can one head learn to match the subject while another attends to punctuation?
options: Each head has its own learned query and key projections
Each head sees a different part of the input sentence
Heads use different activation functions
Each head uses a different softmax temperature chosen by hand
questions.answer: Each head has its own learned query and key projections
questions.explanation: 'By projecting the query and key differently…' All heads see the whole sequence, there are no activation functions in attention, and the scaling is the same √head_dim for every head.

questions.question: In figure 15.7, what do the 'separate partitions of the eventual output vector' correspond to in the code?
questions.answer: The slices of the concatenated tensor contributed by each head: head i occupies features i·head_dim to (i+1)·head_dim − 1 before `output_dense` mixes them.
questions.explanation: Concatenation along axis -1 places head outputs side by side.

questions.question: Can you rewrite the pseudocode correctly from memory and state every intermediate shape?
questions.answer: Self-check against the illustrative code: q,k,v = Dense_i(query/key/value) → (b,t,dh),(b,s,dh),(b,s,dh); scores (b,t,s); head (b,t,dh); concat (b,t,h·dh); Dense.
questions.explanation: Use new variable names inside the loop.

questions.question: Which call performs self-attention with a Keras MultiHeadAttention layer `mha`?
options: mha(query=target, key=source, value=source)
mha(query=source, key=source, value=source)
mha(query=source, key=target, value=target)
mha(query=target, key=target, value=source)
questions.answer: mha(query=source, key=source, value=source)
questions.explanation: Self-attention means the sequence attends to itself, so all three arguments are the same tensor (the page writes it as key=source, value=source, query=source). Option 1 is the cross-attention call at the top of the page; option 3 is cross-attention in the other direction; option 4 mixes keys and values from different sequences, which is not meaningful because keys index the values.

questions.question: How was attention first used in the mid-2010s, according to the page, and what problem did it address?
questions.answer: It was added to RNN encoder-decoder translation models: the encoder and decoder sequence outputs were passed through an attention layer whose output updated the target sequence before prediction. It helped with long-range dependencies that the GRU struggles with.
questions.explanation: This is stated in the first paragraph of 15.3.2. Attention gave a direct path from each target position to all source positions.

questions.question: Explain with the book's example how self-attention can resolve the meaning of "station".
questions.answer: In "The train left the station on time.", self-attention can learn a high score between "station" and "train", so the vector for "train" is summed into the representation of "station". The output vector for "station" is then conditioned on the context and points toward the railway sense rather than radio or space station.
questions.explanation: The weighted sum of value vectors mixes contextual information into each token; the weights are learned.

questions.question: Show why a MultiHeadAttention layer applied to a sequence of length 1 is a linear projection, and what 100 such stacked layers reduce to.
questions.answer: With one token there is one score; softmax over one element equals 1, so the output is $x W_V W_O$, a linear map of x. Stacking 100 such layers gives $x W'_1 W'_2 \cdots W'_{100}$, which equals a single matrix multiplication $x W'$.
questions.explanation: The page states the score matrix is "always a single one" and that 100 layers could be simplified; p.469 completes the sentence: "to a single matrix multiplication!"

questions.question: Why can't we simply replace the RNN layers with MultiHeadAttention layers, according to this page?
options: Attention cannot handle long-range dependencies.
Attention lacks a nonlinear activation; it only combines linear projections of the sequence elements.
Attention can only connect two different sequences.
Attention is too slow to train on GPUs.
questions.answer: Attention lacks a nonlinear activation; it only combines linear projections of the sequence elements.
questions.explanation: The book says we "still need an essential ingredient for any deep neural network—a nonlinear activation function." Option 1 is the opposite of what the page says (attention helps with long-range dependencies). Option 3 is contradicted by self-attention. Option 4 is not claimed; in fact Transformers parallelize well (p.489).

questions.question: In what sense is attention "a very expressive pooling operation"?
questions.answer: Like pooling, it aggregates many vectors into one per output position, but it uses learned, input-dependent weights (from query-key scores) instead of fixed equal weights or a max. It is expressive in how it chooses what to aggregate, yet the aggregated quantities are only linear projections.
questions.explanation: The phrase captures both the strength (flexible, context-dependent mixing) and the limitation (no per-token nonlinear transformation) that the page discusses.

questions.question: Can you predict the shapes of the output and of the attention score matrix when you run self-attention on a batch of shape (32, 20, 256) with num_heads=8?
questions.answer: Output: (32, 20, 256). Scores: (32, 8, 20, 20), one 20×20 matrix per head per example.
questions.explanation: Self-attention produces one vector per input token (projected back to the query feature size by default), and each head scores every token against every token. Beyond the book: Keras returns these scores with return_attention_scores=True.

questions.question: According to the page, what are the respective roles of attention and the feedforward network in a Transformer block?
options: Attention normalizes the sequence; the feedforward network adds positional information.
Attention passes information across the sequence; the feedforward network updates the representation of individual items.
Attention updates individual items; the feedforward network passes information across the sequence.
Both mix information across the sequence, at different scales.
questions.answer: Attention passes information across the sequence; the feedforward network updates the representation of individual items.
questions.explanation: This is stated verbatim on the page. Option 3 swaps the roles; the FFN is applied per token. Option 1 confuses roles with normalization and positional embedding (p.475). Option 4 is wrong because the FFN never mixes positions.

questions.question: With hidden_dim = 256 and num_heads = 8, what is key_dim in listing 15.14? What output shape does the block produce for an input of shape (32, 20, 256)?
questions.answer: key_dim = 256 // 8 = 32. Output shape (32, 20, 256).
questions.explanation: key_dim = hidden_dim // num_heads; feed_forward_2 projects back to hidden_dim and residuals preserve shape.

questions.question: What does `source_mask[:, None, :]` do and why is it needed?
questions.answer: It inserts an axis, turning the (batch, source_length) padding mask into (batch, 1, source_length), which MultiHeadAttention broadcasts over query positions to match the attention score shape and prevent attending to padding.
questions.explanation: p.470 explains that attention_mask is broadcast to (batch_size, target_length, source_length) and that the encoder upranks source_mask for this purpose.

questions.question: Why does the book add a feedforward network after self-attention instead of simply stacking more attention layers?
questions.answer: Attention only combines linear projections; stacked attention layers can collapse (in the length-one case) to a single matrix multiplication. Recurrent cells apply a dense projection plus activation to each token, and the FFN restores that nonlinearity in the simplest way.
questions.explanation: This is the argument spanning p.468 and the top of p.469.

questions.question: Which two ingredients from the ConvNet chapter does the book add to the encoder block?
options: Pooling and strides
Dropout and data augmentation
Normalization and residual connections
Depthwise separable convolutions and batch statistics
questions.answer: Normalization and residual connections
questions.explanation: The page says: "two things we learned to be particularly important when building ConvNets back in chapter 9, normalization and residual connections." The other options are not added in listing 15.14 (dropout is only added in chapter 16, p.498).

questions.question: Why does the listing use LayerNormalization instead of BatchNormalization?
questions.answer: BatchNormalization doesn't work well for sequence data; LayerNormalization normalizes each sequence independently from the other sequences in the batch.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph; p.470 contrasts the axes over which statistics are computed.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write the call() method of TransformerEncoder in the correct order (attention, residual, norm, Dense, Dense, residual, norm)?
questions.answer: residual = x = source; mask = source_mask[:, None, :]; x = self_attention(query=x, key=x, value=x, attention_mask=mask); x = x + residual; x = LN1(x); residual = x; x = FF1(x); x = FF2(x); x = x + residual; x = LN2(x); return x.
questions.explanation: Compare with listing 15.14; the key detail is that the residual is reset after the first normalization.

questions.question: For an input of shape (batch_size, sequence_length, embedding_dim), over which axis does the book's layer_normalization compute its statistics?
options: axis=0
axis=1
axis=-1
axis=(0, 1)
questions.answer: axis=-1
questions.explanation: The annotation reads "we only pool data over the last axis." axis=0 would mix samples (like batch norm); axis=1 would mix tokens of a sequence; (0, 1) would do both.

questions.question: What shape is attention_mask broadcast to, and what shape does the encoder give source_mask?
questions.answer: Broadcast to (batch_size, target_length, source_length); source_mask is upranked to (batch_size, 1, source_length).
questions.explanation: Both shapes are stated on the page; the singleton axis broadcasts across all query positions.

questions.question: Why is LayerNormalization more appropriate than BatchNormalization for sequence data?
questions.answer: BatchNormalization pools statistics over the batch axis, creating interactions between samples; LayerNormalization pools within each sequence separately, so each sample's normalization doesn't depend on other (differently padded, differently long) sequences in the batch.
questions.explanation: The page contrasts the axes and states that per-sequence pooling is more appropriate.

questions.question: Apply the correct layer normalization (divide by standard deviation, ε≈0) to the token vector [2, 4, 6, 8]. What would the book's pseudocode (divide by variance) return instead?
questions.explanation: Deviations are [-3, -1, 1, 3]; variance = (9+1+1+9)/4 = 5. Dividing by 5 instead of √5 yields outputs with variance 0.2, not 1, illustrating the pseudocode's simplification.

questions.question: Why can TransformerEncoder blocks be stacked on top of each other?
options: Because they share weights.
Because their input and output have the same shape.
Because LayerNormalization removes the batch axis.
Because attention_mask is recomputed in every block.
questions.answer: Because their input and output have the same shape.
