questions.explanation: The page says so directly. Blocks do not share weights; LayerNormalization does not change shapes; the mask is the same input, not the reason for stackability.

questions.question: What two attention layers does the decoder block use, according to the start of 15.3.3?
questions.answer: First a self-attention layer over the target sequence (like the encoder); then another MultiHeadAttention layer receiving both the target and the source/encoder output (cross-attention, named on p.471).
questions.explanation: The page says "we can use attention twice"; the sentence is completed on p.471.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why the padding mask has a size-1 axis for the target dimension, and what would go wrong without the mask?
questions.answer: Whether key j is padding doesn't depend on which query is looking, so one row is enough and broadcasts across all queries. Without it, real tokens would mix information from padding vectors into their representations.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the attention_mask paragraph.

questions.question: In listing 15.15's cross-attention call, which tensors serve as query and as key/value?
options: query=source, key=value=x
query=x (target representation), key=value=source
query=key=value=x
query=x, key=x, value=source
questions.answer: query=x (target representation), key=value=source
questions.explanation: The call is cross_attention(query=x, key=source, value=source, attention_mask=mask). Option 1 reverses the roles (output would have source length); option 3 is self-attention; option 4 mixes keys and values from different sequences.

questions.question: Why is this layer called cross-attention?
questions.answer: Because it brings information across the encoder and decoder: decoder (target) positions attend to the encoder's output sequence.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first lines of the page.

questions.question: Explain why the decoder's self-attention needs a causal mask, referring to the book's comparison with a Bidirectional RNN.
questions.answer: The book avoided a Bidirectional RNN decoder because it would let the model see the label it was predicting as a feature. Self-attention is inherently bidirectional: any target position can attend to any other, including later ones that contain the next token. Without a causal mask the model would learn to copy the next token and could not generate novel translations.
questions.explanation: The argument starts on this page and finishes on p.472.

questions.question: Which mask setting does listing 15.15 use for the decoder's self-attention?
options: attention_mask=source_mask[:, None, :]
use_causal_mask=True
No mask
attention_mask=target_mask
questions.answer: use_causal_mask=True
questions.explanation: The self-attention call is self_attention(query=x, key=x, value=x, use_causal_mask=True). The source mask is used in cross-attention; no mask would allow cheating; target_mask does not appear in the listing.

questions.question: In source_mask, what do True and False mean, and where is it used in the decoder?
questions.answer: True marks non-padding tokens, False marks padding. It is reshaped to (batch, 1, source_len) and used as attention_mask for the cross-attention layer.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the listing.

questions.question: For target_len = 12 and source_len = 20, what are the shapes of the per-head attention score matrices in the decoder's self-attention and cross-attention?
questions.answer: Self-attention: 12 × 12 (lower triangle allowed by the causal mask). Cross-attention: 12 × 20 (columns for padded source positions masked).
questions.explanation: Rows correspond to queries (target positions), columns to keys: target positions for self-attention, source positions for cross-attention (p.470 gives the general shape (batch, target_length, source_length)).

questions.question: Can you list the three sublayers of TransformerDecoder in order and say which one(s) use the encoder output and which use a causal mask?
questions.answer: 1) self-attention (causal mask), 2) cross-attention (uses the encoder output and the source padding mask), 3) feedforward network (neither).
questions.explanation: Compare with the callouts of listing 15.15.

questions.question: In the causal mask, what does row i specify?
options: Which positions the token at position i may attend to
Which positions may attend to the token at position i
The attention weights of token i
The padding positions of sequence i in the batch
questions.answer: Which positions the token at position i may attend to
questions.explanation: The book: 'Each row i can be read as a mask for attention for the target token at position i.' Columns (not rows) describe who can see a given token. The mask is 0/1, not weights. Padding is a separate mask.

questions.question: Explain what would go wrong if the decoder's self-attention were left unmasked during training.
questions.answer: Each position could attend to the next input token, which is exactly its label. The model would learn to copy it, getting a very low training loss without learning to translate. At inference, future tokens don't exist, so it couldn't generate novel translations.
questions.explanation: From e03 and p.471.

questions.question: How many query-key pairs are allowed by a causal mask for a target length of 20, compared with no mask?
questions.answer: 20·21/2 = 210 allowed pairs, versus 400 without a mask.
questions.explanation: Lower triangle including the diagonal: T(T+1)/2.

questions.question: What is the exact Keras argument for applying a causal mask in `MultiHeadAttention`, and where is it passed?
questions.answer: `use_causal_mask=True`, passed when calling the layer (e.g. `mha(query=x, key=x, value=x, use_causal_mask=True)`).
questions.explanation: The text prints `use_casual_mask`, a typo. Listing 15.15 on p.471 shows the correct spelling.

questions.question: In Figure 15.8, where does the encoder output enter the decoder?
options: As key and value of the decoder's second (cross-)attention sublayer
As the query of the masked self-attention
Added to the decoder's embedding input
As input to the decoder's feedforward sublayer
questions.answer: As key and value of the decoder's second (cross-)attention sublayer
questions.explanation: The encoder line enters the middle multi-head attention box of the decoder. The query comes from the decoder's own masked self-attention output. In Listing 15.15: `cross_attention(query=x, key=source, value=source)`.

questions.question: In what sense does the causal mask give 'the same effect as our RNN layer', and in what sense is it different?
questions.answer: Same: information flows only forward, so each prediction depends only on earlier tokens. Different: an RNN carries that information through a sequential state, one step at a time, while masked attention lets each position read every earlier position directly, and all positions are computed in parallel.
questions.explanation: The book states the similarity. The difference follows from pp.461-466.

questions.question: Can you redraw Figure 15.8 from memory, naming every sublayer and residual connection?
questions.answer: Self-check: encoder [MHA → add&norm → FFN → add&norm]×N; decoder [masked MHA → add&norm → cross MHA(enc) → add&norm → FFN → add&norm]×N.
questions.explanation: Compare with Listings 15.14 and 15.15.

questions.question: Why must every sublayer in the Transformer block output vectors of size 256 (hidden_dim)?
options: Because residual connections add the sublayer output to its input
Because MultiHeadAttention only supports size 256
Because the vocabulary size is divisible by 256
Because Dropout requires a fixed width
questions.answer: Because residual connections add the sublayer output to its input
questions.explanation: `x = x + residual` requires matching shapes. The FFN therefore expands to 2048 and projects back to 256. The other options are false: MHA supports any size, vocabulary size is irrelevant, and Dropout works on any shape.

questions.question: Verify the 3,840,000 parameters of `embedding_5` and the 3,855,000 of the output Dense layer.
questions.explanation: Embeddings have no bias. Dense layers do.

questions.question: What does `source_mask=source != 0` represent, and which attention layers use it?
questions.answer: A boolean mask that is True for real English tokens and False for padding (id 0). It is used by the encoder's self-attention and the decoder's cross-attention.

questions.question: Why does the summary show two NotEqual layers?
questions.answer: The expression `source != 0` appears twice in Listing 15.16 (for the encoder and for the decoder), and each use on a symbolic tensor creates a separate graph node.
questions.explanation: They compute the same mask. Assigning it to a variable once would leave a single node.

questions.question: Break down the encoder's 1,315,072 parameters into attention, layer norms and feedforward.
questions.explanation: Each attention projection is 256 × 256 + 256 (8 heads × 32 = 256).

questions.question: Before reading p.474, predict a weakness of this model compared with the GRU model.
questions.answer: It has no notion of token order: embeddings, attention and per-token FFNs are all position-independent, so shuffling the words gives the same result. It will likely underperform until positional information is added.
questions.explanation: On p.474 it reaches 58% vs 65% for the RNN, and the authors explain this order blindness.

questions.question: Could you write Listing 15.16 from memory given the encoder and decoder classes?
questions.answer: Self-check: two Inputs, two Embeddings, encoder(source=x, source_mask), decoder(target=x, source=encoder_output, source_mask), Dropout, Dense softmax, Model([source, target], …).
questions.explanation: Compare with the RNN model on p.458 to see the parallel structure.

questions.question: Why does the Transformer of listing 15.16 score lower than the GRU translator?
options: It has too few parameters compared to the GRU model
It has no access to word order, because dense layers and attention treat tokens as a set
Sparse categorical crossentropy is unsuitable for attention models
The causal mask prevents the decoder from seeing the source sentence
questions.answer: It has no access to word order, because dense layers and attention treat tokens as a set
questions.explanation: The page diagnoses the problem as order blindness. Parameter count is not raised as the issue; the loss is the same as for the GRU; and the causal mask applies only to target self-attention, while cross-attention sees the whole source.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count of dense_11 from the summary, given hidden_dim = 256 and vocab_size = 15000.
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has input_dim x units weights plus one bias per unit; this matches the printed 3,855,000.

questions.question: If you randomly shuffled the words of every English source sentence (train and validation), what would happen to this model's accuracy, and what would happen to the GRU model's?
questions.answer: The Transformer's accuracy would stay the same, because it cannot perceive source word order; the GRU's would likely drop, since its step-by-step computation depends on order.
questions.explanation: The book states that the Transformer 'wouldn't notice' rearranged source words. The GRU's final state depends on the order in which tokens are processed, so shuffling destroys information it relies on.

questions.question: What does the 58% accuracy figure measure exactly?
questions.answer: The fraction of target positions where the model correctly predicts the next Spanish word, given the correct previous words (teacher forcing).
questions.explanation: The page defines it as predicting the next word correctly 58% of the time; p.459 explains that this assumes correct previous tokens and is only a crude proxy for translation quality.

questions.question: Which inputs feed transformer_decoder_1 according to the summary?
options: Only embedding_6
The encoder output, the source mask not_equal_5 and embedding_6
embedding_5 and embedding_6
dropout_9 and the encoder output
questions.answer: The encoder output, the source mask not_equal_5 and embedding_6
questions.explanation: The 'Connected to' column lists transformer_encod…, not_equal_5[0][0] and embedding_6[0][0]. embedding_5 feeds the encoder, not the decoder, and dropout_9 comes after the decoder.

questions.question: Why does the book call attention a 'set-processing mechanism'?
questions.answer: Because attention scores depend only on the pairs of token vectors involved, not on their positions, so the result is the same for any ordering of the tokens (outputs are just reordered).
questions.explanation: The page says attention focuses on relationships between pairs of elements and is blind to whether they occur at the beginning, middle or end of the sequence.

questions.question: Before reading p.475, sketch how you would give an attention model access to word order. What problems might arise if you simply appended the integer position to each embedding?
questions.answer: Open answer; a good answer proposes adding a position-dependent vector to each token embedding, and notes that raw integer positions can be large and disrupt the scale of embedding values.
questions.explanation: The next page discusses exactly this: concatenating raw positions is problematic because large integers disrupt the value range, and it proposes learned positional embeddings added to word embeddings.

questions.question: Why does the book reject concatenating the raw position index to each embedding?
options: It would make the model too slow to train
Positions can be large integers that disrupt the embedding's value range, and networks dislike large, discrete inputs
Keras does not support concatenation of integer and float tensors
It would make attention order-blind again
questions.answer: Positions can be large integers that disrupt the embedding's value range, and networks dislike large, discrete inputs
questions.explanation: This is the reason printed on the page. Speed and Keras support are not mentioned (and concatenation after casting is possible), and concatenated positions would actually give attention order information, not remove it.

questions.question: For inputs = [[4, 8, 15, 0, 0]], what does ops.cumsum(ops.ones_like(inputs), axis=-1) - 1 return?
questions.explanation: ones_like gives [[1,1,1,1,1]]; cumsum gives [[1,2,3,4,5]]; subtracting 1 gives the positions 0-4. Padding zeros also get positions; masks handle them downstream.

questions.question: With sequence_length = 20, vocab_size = 15000 and hidden_dim = 256, how many parameters does one PositionalEmbedding layer have?
questions.explanation: The layer holds two Embedding tables without biases: the token table and the position table.

questions.question: Contrast how a GRU and a Transformer with positional embeddings obtain word-order information.
questions.answer: The GRU's computation is order aware because it processes tokens sequentially with a carried state; the Transformer's layers are order-blind, so order is injected into the input vectors themselves by adding position vectors.
questions.explanation: The page's opening paragraph makes exactly this contrast between relying on the layer's computation and injecting positional information into the embedded sequence.

questions.question: What property makes the original paper's cyclic encoding attractive, according to the book?
questions.answer: It uniquely characterizes any integer in a large range using a vector of small values in [-1, 1].
questions.explanation: The book describes values varying cyclically with position, giving a unique, small-valued code for each position.

questions.question: What is a limitation of the learned PositionalEmbedding layer in listing 15.17?
options: It cannot be trained with backpropagation
It changes the embedding dimension from output_dim to output_dim + 1
It has no vectors for positions at or beyond sequence_length
It only works with the TensorFlow backend
questions.answer: It has no vectors for positions at or beyond sequence_length
questions.explanation: position_embeddings is Embedding(sequence_length, output_dim). It is trained by backpropagation, keeps the dimension (it adds), and uses keras.ops, which is backend-agnostic.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why adding position vectors fixes the problem that shuffling source words was invisible to the model (p.474)?
questions.answer: Open answer; after adding position vectors, a shuffled sentence produces different input vectors (each word gets a different position vector), so attention scores and outputs change.
questions.explanation: Permutation equivariance only holds when the same vectors are reordered; positional embeddings make the vector of a word depend on its position, so reordering changes the vectors themselves.

questions.question: What is the essential architectural change from listing 15.16 to listing 15.18?
options: The number of attention heads is doubled
Both Embedding layers are replaced with PositionalEmbedding layers
A GRU layer is added after the encoder
The causal mask is removed from the decoder
questions.answer: Both Embedding layers are replaced with PositionalEmbedding layers
questions.explanation: num_heads stays 8, no GRU is added, and the decoder is unchanged. The only intended change is positional embeddings (the 2056 versus 2048 difference is most likely a typo).

questions.question: Why does the Transformer train about three times faster per epoch than the GRU model?
questions.answer: Attention has no looping state passing, so the whole attention computation can be done in one go on a GPU/TPU, whereas the GRU must process timesteps sequentially.
questions.explanation: The book attributes the speed-up to removing the GRU's looped state passing, and says it would hold even at matched parameter counts.

questions.question: Using the GRU model's 34,869,912 parameters (p.459) and roughly 14.44 million for this model, what fraction of the GRU's parameters does the Transformer use?
questions.answer: About 0.41, i.e. roughly 41%.
questions.explanation: 14,439,064 / 34,869,912 is about 0.414; the book rounds this to 'half'.

questions.question: Is the comparison between the 67% Transformer and the 65% GRU perfectly controlled? Name one difference other than the architecture.
questions.answer: No: the Transformer was trained for 30 epochs, the GRU for 15 (and intermediate_dim changed slightly).
questions.explanation: fit(..., epochs=30) here versus epochs=15 on p.459. The book later notes that the GRU plateaued after about 5 epochs (p.478), so extra epochs would likely not have helped it much.

questions.question: How many percentage points does adding positional embeddings gain over the first Transformer?
questions.explanation: 67% - 58% = 9. 2 is the gain over the GRU (65%), 7 was the GRU's lead over the first Transformer, and 12 matches no comparison.

questions.question: The book says the speed advantage would hold even if parameter counts were matched. Why does parameter count not explain it?
questions.answer: Speed depends on how parallel the computation is, not just on how much there is. The GRU's sequential dependency forces many small steps; attention uses a few large parallel matrix operations.
questions.explanation: A GPU can only exploit parallel work; the RNN's timestep loop is inherently sequential regardless of size.

questions.question: Try training listing 15.18 with intermediate_dim = 2048 and then 2056. Do you expect a measurable difference? Why?
questions.answer: Open answer; a difference of 8 units changes about 8,000 parameters out of 14.4 million, so no meaningful change is expected.
questions.explanation: The FFN size difference is tiny; any difference in accuracy would be within run-to-run noise.

questions.question: Why does Listing 15.19 apply `tokenized_target_sentence[:, :-1]`?
options: To remove the [start] token
Because the Transformer's positional embedding only has sequence_length positions while the Spanish tokenizer outputs sequence_length + 1 tokens
To remove the [end] token before prediction
Because the encoder input is one token shorter than the decoder input
questions.answer: Because the Transformer's positional embedding only has sequence_length positions while the Spanish tokenizer outputs sequence_length + 1 tokens
questions.explanation: The Spanish tokenizer is built with `output_sequence_length=sequence_length + 1` (p.455), and `PositionalEmbedding` has `sequence_length` rows (pp.475-476). [start] is at the front and is not removed by `[:, :-1]`. [end] is never in the prefix while decoding. The encoder input length is not involved.

questions.question: At iteration i, which row of `next_token_predictions` is read, and what does that row represent?
questions.answer: Row i (`[0, i, :]`): the probability distribution over the Spanish vocabulary for the token that follows the i-th token of the current prefix.
questions.explanation: With teacher forcing, the output at position i was trained to predict target token i+1. The prefix has i+1 tokens (positions 0..i), so row i predicts the next one.

questions.question: The decoder input is padded with zeros after the current prefix. Why doesn't this padding change the prediction read at row i?
questions.answer: The decoder's causal self-attention mask prevents position i from attending to any position after i, so the padding to the right is invisible to row i.
questions.explanation: This is the same mask that lets training predict all positions in parallel without leaking future tokens (section 15.3.3).

questions.question: Which statement about the Transformer's speed is correct?
options: It trains and generates in parallel over the whole sequence
It trains in parallel, but greedy generation still needs one forward pass per output token
It generates faster than it trains
Generation is parallel but training requires a loop
questions.answer: It trains in parallel, but greedy generation still needs one forward pass per output token
questions.explanation: p.476 credits the absence of loops for faster training. Listing 15.19 shows generation is still a Python loop of up to 20 `predict` calls. The other options reverse or overstate this.

questions.question: Identify two errors in the translation of "The resemblance between these two men is uncanny."
questions.answer: It inserts "cantantes" (singers), a word not in the source; and it uses "son asombrosa" (plural verb, feminine adjective) where the singular masculine "es asombroso" is required for "el parecido".
questions.explanation: These are typical errors of a small model: a hallucinated token and broken agreement over a longer span.

questions.question: Name one inefficiency in `generate_translation()` and how it could be removed.
questions.answer: The encoder is re-run on the unchanged English sentence at every step (it could be computed once and reused), and the decoder recomputes all previous positions (keys/values could be cached, as chapter 16 does).
questions.explanation: Only row i of a full (1, 20, vocab) output is used per call; p.504 discusses caching for decoder-only models.

questions.question: Without looking, write the loop body of the generation function from memory, including the line that differs from the RNN version.
questions.answer: Tokenize the prefix, slice `[:, :-1]`, predict on `[source, prefix]`, argmax at row i, look up the word, append, break on `[end]`.
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce it and justify the slice, you understand both the decoding loop and the shape constraint of the positional embedding.

questions.question: What evidence from this chapter do the authors give that the Transformer is 'data hungry'?
options: It needed 1,024 GPUs to train
The RNN translator plateaued after about 5 epochs while the Transformer was still improving after 30
It achieved 67% accuracy on the first epoch
It overfit after 2 epochs
questions.answer: The RNN translator plateaued after about 5 epochs while the Transformer was still improving after 30
questions.explanation: That observation is stated on this page. The 1,024 GPUs refer to RoBERTa pretraining (p.480). 67% was the final accuracy, not the first epoch's, and no early overfitting is reported.

questions.question: According to the authors, which parts of the Transformer have been changed by later research?
questions.answer: Attention, normalization and positional embeddings; for very long sequences some models replace attention entirely with something less computationally complex.
questions.explanation: Listed in the second printed paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why does the absence of loops during training help Transformers scale on GPUs/TPUs?
questions.answer: All sequence positions can be computed simultaneously as large matrix operations, whereas an RNN must process time steps one after another. Accelerators are fast at large parallel matrix operations, so more data can be processed per unit of time.
questions.explanation: p.476 measured about 3x faster epochs than the GRU model for this reason.

questions.question: What does the 'E' in BERT stand for, and what does it imply?
options: Embedding: it only learns word embeddings
Encoder: it is the encoder part of a Transformer and produces representations rather than generating text
Ensemble: it combines several Transformers
Evaluation: it is a benchmark
questions.answer: Encoder: it is the encoder part of a Transformer and produces representations rather than generating text
questions.explanation: BERT = Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. p.479 confirms its structure is exactly the encoder half of the translation Transformer and that it is not meant for generation in a loop.

questions.question: What do the authors mean by saying 'the field of machine learning moves empirically', and what example do they give?
questions.answer: Progress comes from experiments and trial and error rather than derivations of optimal designs. Attention grew out of attempts to augment RNNs, and after years of guessing and checking it produced the Transformer.
questions.explanation: This is why the authors say the configuration is not optimal and expect further changes.

questions.question: Can you explain in two sentences why the industry moved toward large pretrained models that 'cost millions to train'?
questions.answer: Transformers train efficiently in parallel and keep improving with more data and parameters, so scaling them up gives much better general text understanding. That one-time cost is then reused across many downstream tasks via fine-tuning.
questions.explanation: If you can connect parallelism, data hunger and reuse, you have the page's main argument.

questions.question: Which conditional distribution does a masked language model learn?
options: p(token | past tokens)
p(token | surrounding tokens)
p(label | tokens)
p(next sentence | sentence)
questions.answer: p(token | surrounding tokens)
questions.explanation: The book contrasts the causal LM's p(token|past tokens) with the MLM's p(token|surrounding tokens). p(label|tokens) is a supervised classifier. Next-sentence prediction was a separate BERT objective that the book does not discuss (and RoBERTa dropped).

questions.question: Roughly what fraction of tokens is replaced by [MASK] in BERT's pretraining, and what is the training target?
questions.answer: About 15%; the target is the original token at each masked position.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why is masked language modeling called unsupervised, and why did that matter for BERT?
questions.answer: The targets are the original tokens, obtained by masking random positions of any text, so no human labels are needed. This allowed collecting the very large amount of text that a 100M-300M parameter model requires.
questions.explanation: The book links model size to data needs and MLM's label-free setup to data availability.

questions.question: What does the book identify as the most notable difference between RoBERTa and BERT?
options: A decoder was added
It uses 10x more training text (160 GB vs. 16 GB)
It uses character-level tokenization
It has 10x more parameters
questions.answer: It uses 10x more training text (160 GB vs. 16 GB)
questions.explanation: RoBERTa made only minor architectural simplifications; the book stresses the extra data and better performance at equal parameter count. It remains encoder-only, uses subword tokenization (p.480), and its base model is BERT-base sized.

questions.question: What does a pretrained Transformer give that pretrained word embeddings from chapter 14 do not?
questions.answer: A representation of each word computed in the context of the surrounding words, so the same word gets different vectors in different sentences.
questions.explanation: Static embeddings map each word to one fixed vector; a Transformer encoder mixes in context through attention.

questions.question: A 512-token sequence is used for MLM with 15% masking. About how many positions contribute to the loss, and how does that compare with a causal LM on the same sequence?
questions.answer: About 77 positions (0.15 × 512 ≈ 76.8). A causal LM gets a prediction target at about 511 positions, so roughly 6-7x more training signal per sequence.
questions.explanation: MLM scores only masked positions. This lower sample efficiency is one reason MLM models need lots of data.

questions.question: Why must you use the matching tokenizer with a pretrained model?
questions.answer: Because token ids index the learned embedding table. If words map to different ids than during pretraining, the model looks up the wrong learned representations.
questions.explanation: This is the first of the requirements listed at the bottom of the page and continued on p.480.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend why BERT is good for classifying movie reviews but not for writing them?
questions.answer: BERT sees the whole review at once through bidirectional attention and was trained to fill in blanks, so it builds rich representations, which is ideal for classification. It never learned to predict the next word from only the past, so it is not suited to generating text token by token.
questions.explanation: Check that your answer mentions bidirectionality and the training objective.

questions.question: Why can't we build our own vocabulary from the IMDb reviews and feed the ids into pretrained RoBERTa?
options: Because IMDb reviews contain too many words for any vocabulary
Because the token ids would not match the ids used in pretraining, so the learned token representations would be wrong
Because RoBERTa only accepts character-level input
Because custom vocabularies cannot be used with Keras models
questions.answer: Because the token ids would not match the ids used in pretraining, so the learned token representations would be wrong
questions.explanation: p480_e03: if the words map to different indices than during pretraining, the learned representations cannot be used. IMDb vocabulary size is not the problem, RoBERTa uses subwords rather than characters, and Keras supports custom vocabularies in general.

questions.question: Name the three things needed to use a pretrained model, according to pp.479-480.
questions.answer: A matching tokenizer, a matching model architecture, and the pretrained weights.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets. KerasHub's from_preset supplies all three.

questions.question: Explain why character-level and word-level tokenization are both poor choices at RoBERTa's scale.
questions.answer: Character tokens make sequences much longer, so training (especially attention) is much more expensive. Word tokens need a huge vocabulary to cover web text, which makes the Embedding layer unworkably large. Subwords keep sequences short with a vocabulary of about 50k.
questions.explanation: This follows p480_e11 directly: it is a trade-off between sequence length and vocabulary size.

questions.question: RoBERTa-base has hidden size 768 and a vocabulary of about 50,000. Approximately how many parameters are in its token embedding matrix, and what fraction of the 124M total is that?
questions.answer: $50{,}000 \times 768 = 38.4$M parameters, about 31% of 124M.
questions.explanation: An embedding matrix has one row of hidden_dim values per vocabulary entry. The 768 width comes from p.481 and the 124M total from p.481's summary.

questions.question: What does `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("roberta_base_en")` return?
options: A sentiment classifier ready to predict IMDb labels
The RoBERTa-base architecture with pretrained weights, outputting per-token features
Only the tokenizer vocabulary
An untrained RoBERTa with random weights
questions.answer: The RoBERTa-base architecture with pretrained weights, outputting per-token features
questions.explanation: from_preset loads weights, configuration and assets. A Backbone has no task head (p.481), so it is not a classifier. The tokenizer is loaded separately, and the weights are pretrained, not random.

questions.question: `tokenizer("The quick brown fox")` returns four ids. What does this tell you about how subword tokenizers handle common words?
questions.answer: Common words are kept as single tokens; only rare words are split into several subword pieces.
questions.explanation: Each of the four common English words maps to one id, so sequence length stays close to word count for typical text.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague, without notes, what a 'backbone' is and why KerasHub separates it from task heads?
questions.answer: A backbone maps inputs to latent features without a prediction head; separating it lets one pretrained body be reused for many tasks by adding small task-specific heads.
questions.explanation: p480_e13 and p.481 define the backbone through the computer-vision analogy from chapter 8 and the screwdriver analogy.

questions.question: What is the output shape of the RoBERTa backbone?
options: (batch_size, 768)
(batch_size, sequence_length, 768)
(batch_size, 2)
(batch_size, sequence_length, 50000)
questions.answer: (batch_size, sequence_length, 768)
questions.explanation: p481_e03 states this shape: one 768-d vector per token. (batch, 768) would need pooling, (batch, 2) is a classifier output, and (batch, seq, vocab) would be a masked-LM head.

questions.question: Verify the per-layer count 7,087,872 given hidden size 768 and feedforward size 3,072.
questions.explanation: Multi-head attention has query, key, value and output projections, each d×d plus bias. The FFN has two Dense layers, and each LayerNorm has a scale and an offset of size d.

questions.question: Using the summary, check that the total is 124,052,736 and that it occupies about 473 MB in float32.
questions.explanation: Dropout and the inputs have no parameters. Keras' 'MB' divides by 2^20.

questions.question: Why does every transformer_layer in the summary connect to padding_mask?
questions.answer: Each layer's self-attention must ignore padding positions, so the mask is passed to every layer, not only the first.
questions.explanation: Padding tokens are added to reach a fixed length (p.482-483). Without the mask, real tokens would attend to padding at every layer.

questions.question: What does the screwdriver analogy describe?
questions.answer: A single backbone fitted with different task-specific heads (for example, a classification head for IMDb), as you fit different heads to one screwdriver.
questions.explanation: p481_e04: Phillips head for one task, flat head for another.

questions.question: Which part of RoBERTa-base has the most parameters?
options: The embedding layer
The 12 encoder layers taken together
The embedding layer norm
The padding mask input
questions.answer: The 12 encoder layers taken together
questions.explanation: 12 × 7.09M = 85.1M, against 39.0M for the embeddings. The layer norm has 1,536 parameters and the inputs have none. A single encoder layer, however, is smaller than the embedding layer.

questions.question: Can you name three downstream tasks that the same backbone could serve, and say how each would use the per-token outputs?
questions.answer: Sentence classification (pool, then Dense), span identification (per-token start/end scores), part-of-speech tagging (per-token class).
questions.explanation: These are the three examples in p481_e03; the head determines how the features are used.

questions.question: How many reviews end up in the training, validation and test datasets, and how is the 5,000 obtained?
questions.answer: 20,000 train, 5,000 validation, 25,000 test. 20% of each class's 12,500 training files (2,500 × 2) moves to validation.
questions.explanation: val_percentage = 0.2 is applied per category; the test directory is copied whole.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `random.Random(1337).shuffle(src_files)`?
options: To augment the reviews with random noise
To produce the same random train/validation split every run, matching chapter 14
To balance positive and negative classes
To shuffle batches during training
questions.answer: To produce the same random train/validation split every run, matching chapter 14
questions.explanation: A seeded shuffle gives a reproducible split. It does not change the text, class balance comes from splitting each class separately, and batch shuffling is done by text_dataset_from_directory.

questions.question: Why must the reviews be packed with <s> at the start and </s> at the end, instead of just being tokenized?
questions.answer: RoBERTa was pretrained on sequences in this layout. Matching it gives inputs like those the model learned from, so fine-tuning is faster and more accurate, and the <s> position carries the learned summary representation.
questions.explanation: p482_e07 and p.483: 'It's important to match the token ordering used for pretraining as closely as possible.'

questions.question: Name two differences between this code and chapter 14's 'unchanged' version.
questions.answer: batch_size is 16 instead of 32, and copytree/makedirs use dirs_exist_ok/exist_ok=True; the copy loop also uses enumerate with if/else.
questions.explanation: Compare with Listings 14.8-14.10 on pp.420-421 and the dataset code on p.422.

questions.question: What does each element of `train_ds` contain?
options: Integer token ids and a padding mask
A batch of 16 raw review strings and their integer labels
One-hot encoded reviews
RoBERTa embeddings of the reviews
questions.answer: A batch of 16 raw review strings and their integer labels
questions.explanation: text_dataset_from_directory reads files and infers labels from folder names. Tokenization and packing happen later in preprocess() (p.483), and embeddings are computed by the backbone.

questions.question: Could you sketch the directory layout that text_dataset_from_directory expects, and explain how labels are assigned?
questions.answer: root/neg/*.txt and root/pos/*.txt; labels are assigned from the alphabetical order of the subfolders (neg = 0, pos = 1).
questions.explanation: The split code creates exactly this layout for imdb_train and imdb_val, and the copied imdb_test already has it.

questions.question: What does `StartEndPacker` NOT do in Listing 15.21?
options: Prepend the start token
Append the end token
Pad or truncate to 512 tokens
Convert raw text into token ids
questions.answer: Convert raw text into token ids
questions.explanation: Tokenization is done by `tokenizer(text)`; the packer receives the ids. The book says the packer appends start, end and padding tokens and trims long sequences to a given length.

questions.question: From the printed batch, what are the token ids of <s>, </s> and <pad> in RoBERTa?
questions.explanation: Every row starts with 0; padded rows end with 1s where the mask is False; full rows end with 2.

questions.question: Why do the authors insist on matching the token ordering used during pretraining?
questions.answer: The pretrained weights (position embeddings, attention patterns, the meaning of position 0) were learned for that format; matching it means fine-tuning only has to learn the task, so the model trains more quickly and accurately.
questions.explanation: The book states the speed and accuracy benefit; the mechanism is that the inputs stay in the distribution the weights were trained on.

questions.question: A row of `padding_mask` is all True. What does that tell you about the review?
options: It is empty
It had at least enough tokens to fill 512 positions and was truncated
It is a negative review
It contains only special tokens
questions.answer: It had at least enough tokens to fill 512 positions and was truncated
questions.explanation: No padding means the packed sequence is full; the matching `token_ids` rows end with `</s>` = 2 after real content. Sentiment is unrelated, and an empty review would be mostly padding.

questions.question: Why must the keys of the dict returned by `preprocess` be exactly "token_ids" and "padding_mask"?
questions.answer: They are the names of the RoBERTa backbone's two input layers, and Keras routes dict inputs to model inputs by name.
questions.explanation: See the backbone summary on p.481.

questions.question: A review tokenizes to 200 subword tokens. After packing to 512, how many positions are padding, and what fraction of the padding_mask is True?
questions.answer: 200 + 2 special tokens = 202 real positions; 512 − 202 = 310 padding positions; 202/512 ≈ 39.5% True.
questions.explanation: `<s>` and `</s>` count as real (unmasked) tokens.

questions.question: Could you write `preprocess` from memory and explain each argument of `StartEndPacker`?
questions.answer: sequence_length (512), start_value/end_value/pad_value from the tokenizer, return_padding_mask=True; return ({token_ids, padding_mask}, label).
questions.explanation: If you can also explain the printed batch, you understand the input contract of the pretrained backbone.

questions.question: Which pooling strategy do the authors choose for the IMDb classifier, and why?
options: Mean pooling, because it uses every token equally
Max pooling, because it captures the strongest features
The first token's representation, because attention lets that position gather information from the whole sequence contextually
The last token's representation, because it has seen all previous tokens
questions.answer: The first token's representation, because attention lets that position gather information from the whole sequence contextually
questions.explanation: The book says first-token pooling works slightly better than mean/max pooling because position 0 in the final layer attends to all positions. The last-token rationale applies to causal models, not to a bidirectional encoder.

questions.question: What is the shape of the RoBERTa backbone's output, and what does each 768-d vector represent?
questions.answer: (batch_size, sequence_length, 768); each vector represents one input token in the context of its surrounding words.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of 15.4.4; consistent with the summary on p.481.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, how was GPT-2's training dataset collected?
options: From English Wikipedia and self-published books
By following outgoing links from Reddit
From an English-German translation dataset
From 15 trillion tokens of publicly available sources
questions.answer: By following outgoing links from Reddit
questions.explanation: Wikipedia + books is BERT, translation pairs are the original Transformer, and 15T tokens is Llama.

questions.question: Why do the authors advise paying attention to where a model's pretraining data came from?
questions.answer: Because the data shapes the model's biases and performance, and the exact data mixture matters a lot (shown in the next chapter), while companies increasingly keep it vague.
questions.explanation: From the closing paragraph of the sidebar.

questions.question: For a batch of shape (16, 512, 768), what are the output shapes after (a) `x[:, 0, :]` and (b) mean pooling over the sequence axis? How many token vectors does each reduction consider?
questions.answer: (a) (16, 768), reading only position 0 directly (which already mixes all positions through attention). (b) (16, 768), averaging up to 512 vectors per sample (only the unmasked ones if done correctly).
questions.explanation: Both reduce the sequence axis; they differ in how the aggregation weights are determined.

questions.question: Why does first-token pooling make sense for RoBERTa specifically, given the preprocessing on p.483?
questions.answer: StartEndPacker puts `<s>` at position 0 of every review, so the first position is always the same content-free token, whose final vector is purely an attention-built summary of the review.
questions.explanation: Consistent packing guarantees position 0 plays the same role for every sample.

questions.question: Can you list the four example pretraining datasets in chronological order and describe the trend they illustrate?
questions.answer: Original Transformer (4M translation pairs) → BERT (Wikipedia + 7,000 books) → GPT-2 (Reddit-linked web pages) → Llama (15T tokens, vaguely described). Trend: rapidly growing scale, more web scraping, less transparency.
questions.explanation: If you can name the trend in three words (bigger, webbier, vaguer), you have the sidebar's message.

questions.question: What does `x = x[:, 0, :]` do in Listing 15.22?
options: Keeps the first review of each batch
Keeps the hidden vector of the first token of each sequence
Averages the hidden vectors over all tokens
Keeps the first feature of every token vector
questions.answer: Keeps the hidden vector of the first token of each sequence
questions.explanation: The backbone output has shape (batch, sequence, 768). Indexing 0 on axis 1 selects the first token for every example, as the callout says. Axis 0 would be the batch (first review), averaging would be mean pooling, and indexing the last axis would pick a single feature.

questions.question: How many epochs does Listing 15.23 train for, and how can you tell?
questions.answer: One epoch: `fit()` is called without an `epochs` argument, and Keras defaults to 1; the text confirms 'In just a single epoch of training'.
questions.explanation: The default value of `epochs` in `Model.fit()` is 1, which matches the authors' statement.

questions.question: Why is the learning rate set to 5e-5 instead of Adam's default 1e-3 when fine-tuning RoBERTa?
questions.answer: The backbone's weights already encode valuable knowledge from pretraining; large updates (especially while the new head is still random and produces large, noisy gradients) could destroy it. A small learning rate adapts the representations gently.
questions.explanation: This is the essence of fine-tuning versus training from scratch; the book uses 5e-5 without discussing it, so the reasoning here is an explanation beyond the page.

questions.question: The test output is `[0.168127179145813, 0.9366399645805359]`. If the test set has 25,000 reviews, roughly how many were misclassified? And what geometric-mean probability of the correct label does a loss of 0.168 correspond to?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction correct, so errors = 25,000 × 0.06336. Binary cross-entropy averages $-\ln p_{\text{correct}}$, so exponentiating the negative mean loss gives the geometric mean of $p_{\text{correct}}$. (The 25,000 figure is the standard IMDb test size, an assumption here.)

questions.question: According to the page, what is the main downside of the RoBERTa classifier compared with chapter 14's bigram model?
options: It needs more labeled data
It is far more expensive to use
It cannot handle unseen words
It needs many epochs to converge
questions.answer: It is far more expensive to use
questions.explanation: The authors say 'this is a far more expensive model to use than the simple bigram classifier'. It used the same labeled data, the subword tokenizer handles any word (p.480), and it converged in one epoch.

questions.question: What was Word2Vec's training objective, as described at the start of section 15.5?
questions.answer: To turn correlation relationships between words into distance relationships: each word gets a vector, optimized so that vectors of frequently co-occurring words have a dot-product (cosine proximity) close to 1 and those of rarely co-occurring words close to 0.
questions.explanation: The first half of this is on this page; the 'close to 0' half finishes the sentence on p.486.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why fine-tuned RoBERTa beats chapter 14's LSTM by about 10 points of accuracy on the same data?
questions.answer: Self-check: mention that the LSTM had to learn embeddings from 20,000 reviews and overfitted before learning good ones (p.437), while RoBERTa arrives with representations learned from 160 GB of text (p.479) and only needs to adapt them.
questions.explanation: If you can connect the result to the data-hunger argument of chapter 14, you understand why pretraining matters.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the answer to the question 'How does the language model loss function relate to Word2Vec's objective of maximizing the dot-product between co-occurring tokens?'
options: The positional embedding
The attention mechanism
The feedforward layers
The softmax output layer
questions.answer: The attention mechanism
questions.explanation: The text says outright: 'The answer is the attention mechanism.' Attention recombines embeddings weighted by dot-product closeness, which pulls co-occurring tokens together. Positional embeddings add word-order information (p.475). Feedforward layers and the output softmax process tokens one at a time and do not mix information across tokens.

questions.question: With toy vectors king=(0.9, 0.8), man=(0.1, 0.8), woman=(0.1, 0.1), compute V(king) - V(man) + V(woman). Then find its cosine similarity to queen=(0.9, 0.1).
questions.answer: (0.9, 0.1); cosine similarity 1.0
questions.explanation: (0.9-0.1+0.1, 0.8-0.8+0.1) = (0.9, 0.1), which is identical to queen, so the cosine is 1. In real embeddings the result is only *near* queen, and queen is chosen as the nearest neighbour.

questions.question: Name the four similarities the authors list between Word2Vec and Transformers.
questions.answer: Both embed tokens (words or subwords) in a vector space; both learn the space on the principle that co-occurring tokens end up close; both compare tokens with cosine distance; both use embedding vectors of similar dimensionality.
questions.explanation: These come straight from the 'Both models seek to embed tokens…' paragraph. Note that the stated range of 1,000-10,000 dimensions is inaccurate for Word2Vec (usually 300).

questions.question: Why would giving more weight to tokens that already have a higher dot-product tend to pull those tokens even closer together?
questions.answer: Each token's new vector is a weighted average dominated by its similar neighbours. When two similar tokens each mix in a large share of the other, their new vectors are more alike than before, while dissimilar tokens barely mix.
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces differences between the things averaged. With dot-product weights, the averaging is concentrated among already-similar tokens, so correlation becomes proximity, as the page claims.

questions.question: Which statement describes 'semantically interpolative' as defined on the page?
options: Small moves in the space change meaning only slightly
The midpoint between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning
Each token has exactly one fixed vector
Distances are measured with L2 rather than cosine
questions.answer: The midpoint between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning
questions.explanation: The second bullet defines interpolation as the intermediate point producing an 'intermediate meaning'. The first option is semantic continuity, the other property. Fixed vectors describe Word2Vec, not Transformer layers. The page names cosine, not L2.

questions.question: In what sense is a Transformer 'a series of incrementally refined embedding spaces'?
questions.answer: Each attention block takes the previous layer's token vectors and outputs new vectors built by recombining them, so every layer defines a new, more contextual embedding space for the next layer.
questions.explanation: This paraphrases the page's final sentence about attention. Unlike Word2Vec's single static table, the representation of each token changes layer by layer.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend, without equations, why Word2Vec's 'gender vector' was surprising and how it foreshadows what the authors say about Transformers?
questions.answer: Self-assessment: it was surprising because the model was only trained on co-occurrence, yet one consistent direction encoded gender for many word pairs. It foreshadows the claim that Transformers learn far richer 'functions' (vector programs, p.487) as a by-product of organizing tokens in space.
questions.explanation: If you can link 'emergent direction' to 'emergent function', you have the thread that runs from this page to p.487.

questions.question: According to the authors, why are the embedding spaces learned by a Transformer semantically interpolative?
options: Because positional embeddings are sinusoidal
Because each new embedding space is built by interpolating between vectors from the previous space
Because the vocabulary uses subword tokens
Because the model is trained with dropout
questions.answer: Because each new embedding space is built by interpolating between vectors from the previous space
questions.explanation: The first sentence on the page gives this reason. Positional encodings, subword tokenization and dropout are unrelated to the interpolation claim.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'neurons that fire together, wire together' summarize, and how do the authors relate it to Transformers?
questions.answer: Hebbian learning: correlations between neural firing events become stronger connections, i.e. proximity in the brain network. Transformers and Word2Vec likewise turn correlation relationships into vector proximity relationships.
questions.explanation: The authors conclude that both are 'maps of a space of information'. The analogy concerns the outcome, not the training algorithm.

questions.question: The authors compare Word2Vec to 'a logistic regression on MNIST pixels'. What point does that comparison make?
questions.answer: The fundamental principles are mostly the same as in state-of-the-art models, but the toy model lacks meaningful representation power: Word2Vec is shallow and single-layer, unlike billion-parameter, many-layer Transformers.
questions.explanation: Logistic regression on raw pixels and modern vision models both classify images by learned functions, but the gap in capacity is huge. The same holds for Word2Vec vs. Transformers.

questions.question: Which is an example of a 'vector program' that only a large Transformer, not Word2Vec, could perform?
options: plural(cat) → cats
male_to_female(king) → queen
write_this_in_style_of_shakespeare("...your poem...") → "...new poem..."
V(king) - V(man) + V(woman)
questions.answer: write_this_in_style_of_shakespeare("...your poem...") → "...new poem..."
questions.explanation: The page gives the Shakespeare restyling as the Transformer example. The plural and male_to_female examples are Word2Vec's linear transformations, and the last option is the gender-vector arithmetic from p.486.

questions.question: Explain why the authors say you can 'retrieve a lot more from your database than you put into it', and what the downside is.
questions.answer: Data is stored as a continuous vector space, so you can move to nearby points and interpolate between stored points, producing content never explicitly stored. The downside is that not all of it is accurate or meaningful: interpolation gives generalization but also hallucinations.
questions.explanation: This is the first of the two differences between a Transformer and a database.

questions.question: Besides representation power, what other factor do the authors credit for Transformers going beyond linear transformations?
questions.answer: A much more refined autoregressive optimization objective.
questions.explanation: The text says: 'thanks to this increased representation power and a much more refined autoregressive optimization objective, we're no longer confined to linear transformations'.

questions.question: Can you state both differences between a Transformer and a database (the second finishes on p.488)?
questions.answer: Self-check: (1) it is continuous and interpolative rather than a set of discrete entries; (2) it contains not just data but, perhaps primarily, programs.
questions.explanation: If you could only recall the first, read the top of p.488.

questions.question: Which distribution does a masked language model learn, according to the summary?
options: p(token|past tokens)
p(tokens|surrounding tokens)
p(source|target)
p(label|tokens)
questions.answer: p(tokens|surrounding tokens)
questions.explanation: That is the masked LM bullet. p(token|past tokens) is the causal LM. The other two are not described as language-model distributions in the summary (a classifier head learns labels, but that is fine-tuning).

questions.question: How do vector programs differ from Python programs, according to the authors?
questions.answer: Python programs are series of symbolic statements processing data step by step. Vector programs are highly nonlinear functions that map the latent embedding space onto itself, like Word2Vec's magic vectors but far more complex.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the second paragraph of the page.

questions.question: What do the authors mean by calling LLMs 'fundamentally interpolative', and what limit do they draw from it?
questions.answer: Thanks to attention, LLMs learn an interpolative embedding space over a large share of written English and produce outputs by wandering and blending within it. This can give unexpected generalizations, but it cannot synthesize something fundamentally new with genuine human-level intelligence.
questions.explanation: It ties together the interpolation property (p.486) and the database view (p.487) as a statement about the limits of capability. It is the authors' position.

questions.question: In a seq2seq model, what does the decoder use to predict the next target token?
options: Only the source sequence
Only past target tokens
The encoder's representation of the source and the past target tokens
Future target tokens
questions.answer: The encoder's representation of the source and the past target tokens
questions.explanation: The summary says the decoder takes the encoder's representation as input and predicts the next target token based on past tokens. Using only one of them would be a plain encoder or a plain LM, and future tokens are masked out.

questions.question: A query q=(1,0) attends to keys k1=(2,0) and k2=(0,2) (no scaling). Compute the softmax attention weights.
questions.answer: Scores 2 and 0; weights e^2/(e^2+1) ≈ 0.881 and 1/(e^2+1) ≈ 0.119.
questions.explanation: The dot-product scores are q·k1=2 and q·k2=0. Softmax gives most weight to the key closer to the query, which illustrates 'vectors near each other … will be summed together'.

questions.question: What problem of RNNs does attention avoid, according to the summary?
questions.answer: Problems with long-range dependencies in text.
questions.explanation: Attention connects any two positions directly, instead of carrying information through many recurrent steps.

questions.question: Without looking, write the three language-model distributions (causal, masked, seq2seq) and one application of each.
questions.answer: Self-check: p(token|past tokens), text generation; p(tokens|surrounding tokens), classification; p(next target token | past target tokens, source), translation or question answering.
questions.explanation: If any is fuzzy, revisit pp.445, 479 and 452.

questions.question: According to the chapter summary, what is the only mechanism a Transformer uses to pass information across a sequence?
options: Recurrence
Convolution
Attention
Positional embeddings
questions.answer: Attention
questions.explanation: The summary states attention is the only such mechanism. Recurrence belongs to RNNs, convolution is not used, and positional embeddings add order information to each token but do not move information between positions.

questions.question: Why does the absence of sequence-length loops make Transformers easier to train in parallel than RNNs?
questions.answer: An RNN must compute each hidden state from the previous one, so time steps are sequential. A Transformer processes all positions with matrix products in one pass, so the work can be spread across many cores and machines.
questions.explanation: This is the third sub-point of the summary bullet; the matrix-product detail is an explanation beyond the page.

questions.question: Which kind of attention does a Transformer decoder use to predict the next word?
options: Bidirectional attention
Causal attention
Cross-attention only
No attention
questions.answer: Causal attention
questions.explanation: The decoder must not see future tokens, so its self-attention is causal. Bidirectional attention is the encoder's; cross-attention is an additional sublayer in seq2seq decoders, not the next-word mechanism by itself.

questions.question: What two sublayers alternate inside each Transformer block, according to the summary?
questions.answer: An attention layer and a two-layer feedforward network.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sub-point; residual connections and normalization also appear in the blocks built on pp.468-471.

questions.question: Why would a bidirectional encoder like RoBERTa be a poor choice for generating text left to right?
questions.answer: It was trained with access to both left and right context; when generating, the right context does not exist yet, and nothing in its training taught it to predict the next token from the past alone.
questions.explanation: The summary pairs encoders with representations and decoders with next-word prediction; p.479 calls the encoder 'not a model meant to run generation in a loop'.

questions.question: Without looking back, can you list the five sub-points of the Transformer bullet and give one page where each was introduced?
questions.answer: Self-check: block structure (p.468), scaling (p.484 and section 15.4), no sequence loops (vs RNNs, p.456), bidirectional encoder (p.479), causal decoder (p.470).
questions.explanation: Being able to tie each claim to the chapter's code shows you have consolidated chapter 15 before starting chapter 16.
